Chapter 9 Differential item functioning and fairness Learning goals. After this chapter you can tell impact (a real difference between groups) from DIF (an item that works differently for people of the same ability); run an IRT likelihood-ratio DIF analysis and read its effect sizes; distinguish uniform from non-uniform DIF; run a Mantel-Haenszel DIF test and classify items with the ETS A/B/C rules; explain why anchor items matter. Key terms: DIF, reference and focal groups, uniform and non-uniform DIF, DIF effect size, anchor items. 9.1 The ideas Groups often differ in their average scores. That alone says nothing about whether a test is fair: The groups may simply differ in what the test measures, which is called impact. An item shows differential item functioning (DIF) when people from different groups with the same ability have different chances of answering it correctly (Holland and Wainer 1993). DIF is a statistical finding, not a verdict of bias; a content review decides whether the reason is irrelevant to what the test should measure (bias) or a real difference in what was taught. We compare a reference group (often the majority group) with a focal group. In IRT terms, DIF means the item has different parameters in the two groups. Uniform DIF: The item is harder for one group at every ability level (the difficulty differs, the curves are parallel). Non-uniform DIF: The size or direction of the difference changes with ability (the slopes differ and the curves cross). To compare groups we must first put them on a common scale, and that needs items we trust to work the same way in both: The anchors. mirtverse’s dif() uses a constrained-baseline approach: It fits a multiple-group model in which all item parameters are equal across groups while the group means and variances are free, then frees each item’s parameters in turn and tests the change with a likelihood-ratio test. Items you do not test serve as anchors. Because each test involves only one free item, the approach works well when DIF is confined to a few items; when many items have DIF, a purification step (testing, removing flagged items from the anchor set, and testing again) is safer. A significant test is not enough: With large samples tiny differences are significant. dif() therefore reports effect sizes on the item score scale. The signed version (esd) is the average difference in the probability of a correct answer between the focal and the reference group at the same ability; the unsigned version (uesd) also captures crossing curves. The Mantel-Haenszel (MH) procedure (Holland and Thayer 1988) is the classical alternative. It matches people on their sum score, builds a 2 × 2 table (group × right/wrong) at every score level and tests whether the odds of a correct answer differ between groups across the tables. ETS classifies the size of MH DIF as A (negligible), B (moderate) or C (large). 9.2 Example 1: Paper versus tablet A district moved its Grade 5 reading test from paper to tablets. We simulate 25 items answered by 1,200 students on paper (reference) and 800 on tablets (focal). The tablet group is slightly weaker on average (impact). Two items that ask students to drag text into a table are harder on tablets (uniform DIF), and one long-passage item is easier for strong tablet readers and harder for weak ones (non-uniform DIF). # Simulated 25-item reading test; `group` is the test mode for each student. set.seed(909) a <- matrix(rlnorm(25, 0.2, 0.25)); d <- matrix(rnorm(25, 0.2, 0.9)) a_tab <- a; d_tab <- d d_tab[c(7, 18)] <- d[c(7, 18)] - 0.8 # R07, R18: uniform DIF a_tab[22] <- a[22] * 1.8; d_tab[22] <- d[22] # R22: non-uniform DIF paper <- simdata(a, d, N = 1200, itemtype = "2PL") tablet <- simdata(a_tab, d_tab, N = 800, itemtype = "2PL", Theta = matrix(rnorm(800, -0.2, 1))) resp <- rbind(paper, tablet) colnames(resp) <- sprintf("R%02d", 1:25) group <- factor(rep(c("Paper", "Tablet"), c(1200, 800)), levels = c("Paper", "Tablet")) The raw scores differ between the groups, but that alone does not tell us which items, if any, are unfair: mode_resp <- resp; mode_group <- group # kept for the exercises tapply(rowSums(resp), group, mean) #> Paper Tablet #> 12.6 11.1 dif() tests every item. Paper is the reference group because it is the first level of the factor. res <- dif(resp, group = group) res #> DIF analysis: Paper (reference) vs Tablet; 25 items tested #> Likelihood-ratio tests freeing a1, d; BH-adjusted p < 0.05 flags DIF #> #> item X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag esd uesd converged #> R01 1.273 2 .529 .758 -0.007 0.018 TRUE #> R02 2.153 2 .341 .758 0.016 0.022 TRUE #> R03 0.264 2 .876 .876 0.005 0.009 TRUE #> R04 1.480 2 .477 .758 -0.022 0.022 TRUE #> R05 1.158 2 .560 .758 0.011 0.019 TRUE #> R06 0.953 2 .621 .758 -0.017 0.018 TRUE #> R07 29.459 2 < .001 < .001 DIF -0.100 0.100 TRUE #> R08 1.447 2 .485 .758 0.021 0.024 TRUE #> R09 1.793 2 .408 .758 -0.019 0.021 TRUE #> R10 5.327 2 .070 .290 0.013 0.044 TRUE #> R11 4.878 2 .087 .312 0.041 0.041 TRUE #> R12 7.665 2 .022 .108 0.041 0.047 TRUE #> R13 0.720 2 .698 .758 0.001 0.014 TRUE #> R14 1.044 2 .593 .758 0.018 0.018 TRUE #> R15 0.578 2 .749 .780 -0.007 0.012 TRUE #> R16 0.783 2 .676 .758 -0.011 0.013 TRUE #> R17 9.572 2 .008 .052 0.061 0.061 TRUE #> R18 45.538 2 < .001 < .001 DIF -0.135 0.135 TRUE #> R19 2.351 2 .309 .758 0.017 0.024 TRUE #> R20 1.087 2 .581 .758 -0.006 0.018 TRUE #> R21 1.270 2 .530 .758 0.002 0.019 TRUE #> R22 32.166 2 < .001 < .001 DIF 0.043 0.075 TRUE #> R23 4.298 2 .117 .364 0.028 0.032 TRUE #> R24 0.878 2 .645 .758 0.012 0.015 TRUE #> R25 1.456 2 .483 .758 0.024 0.024 TRUE The flagged items are the three we planted. The signed effect sizes of R07 and R18 are negative, meaning the items are harder for tablet users of the same ability. The baseline model also estimates the impact: The latent mean of the tablet group relative to the paper group (fixed at 0). coef(res$baseline, simplify = TRUE)$Tablet$means #> F1 #> -0.283 9.2.1 Choosing anchors If we already know some items are clean, we can test only the others: The untested items become anchors. Here, as a check, we test only the three flagged items against the other 22: dif(resp, group = group, items = c("R07", "R18", "R22"))$table #> # A tibble: 3 × 9 #> item X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag esd uesd converged #> <chr> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> #> 1 R07 29.5 2 4.01e- 7 4.01e- 7 TRUE -0.0997 0.0997 TRUE #> 2 R18 45.5 2 1.29e-10 3.88e-10 TRUE -0.135 0.135 TRUE #> 3 R22 32.2 2 1.04e- 7 1.55e- 7 TRUE 0.0430 0.0755 TRUE Does the DIF matter for scores? One way to judge is to compare the expected total score of the test in the two groups at the same ability, which is called differential test functioning. With two items that are harder for tablet users and one that crosses, the total effect is a fraction of a score point; a content review would still look at the drag-and-drop items, because the problem can be fixed by changing the interface. 9.3 Example 2: Mantel-Haenszel on a chemistry quiz The MH test needs no IRT model, which makes it a good first screen and a useful check. We simulate a 20-item chemistry quiz taken by 600 girls and 600 boys of equal average ability; item C11 involves a sports context and is easier for boys of the same ability. # Simulated 20-item quiz; `group` is gender. C11 has uniform DIF. set.seed(910) a <- matrix(rlnorm(20, 0.2, 0.2)); d <- matrix(rnorm(20, 0, 0.8)) d_boys <- d; d_boys[11] <- d[11] + 0.7 resp <- rbind(simdata(a, d, N = 600, itemtype = "2PL"), simdata(a, d_boys, N = 600, itemtype = "2PL")) colnames(resp) <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:20) group <- factor(rep(c("Girl", "Boy"), each = 600), levels = c("Girl", "Boy")) For each item we match on the total score of the other items, build the stratified 2 × 2 tables and run the MH test. The common odds ratio \(\alpha_{MH}\) converts to the ETS delta scale as \(\text{MH D-DIF} = -2.35 \ln \alpha_{MH}\). The ETS rules call DIF negligible (A) when \(|\text{MH D-DIF}| < 1\) or the test is not significant, large (C) when \(|\text{MH D-DIF}| \ge 1.5\) and significant, and moderate (B) otherwise (the full rules also test the size against 1). mh_item <- function(resp, group, item) { rest <- rowSums(resp[, colnames(resp) != item]) strata <- cut(rest, unique(quantile(rest, 0:5 / 5)), include.lowest = TRUE) tab <- table(group, factor(resp[, item], levels = 1:0), strata) mh <- mantelhaen.test(tab, exact = FALSE) delta <- -2.35 * log(unname(mh$estimate)) data.frame(item = item, alpha_MH = unname(mh$estimate), MH_D_DIF = delta, p.value = mh$p.value, ETS = ifelse(mh$p.value >= 0.05 | abs(delta) < 1, "A", ifelse(abs(delta) >= 1.5, "C", "B"))) } mh <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(resp), mh_item, resp = resp, group = group)) mh[order(mh$p.value), ][1:5, ] #> item alpha_MH MH_D_DIF p.value ETS #> 11 C11 0.576 1.297 3.55e-05 B #> 4 C04 1.288 -0.596 4.54e-02 A #> 13 C13 0.789 0.556 1.22e-01 A #> 1 C01 1.222 -0.471 1.36e-01 A #> 9 C09 1.224 -0.476 1.42e-01 A The table is arranged so that \(\alpha_{MH}\) is the odds of a correct answer in the reference group (girls) divided by the odds in the focal group (boys), at the same score. Values above 1, and negative MH D-DIF, mean the item favours the reference group; values below 1, and positive MH D-DIF, favour the focal group. C11 stands out, with a moderate (B) DIF in favour of boys. Matching on five score bands keeps the tables reasonably full in a sample of this size; with more people you can match on every score. The IRT analysis agrees: subset(dif(resp, group = group)$table, flag) #> # A tibble: 1 × 9 #> item X2 df p.value p.adjusted flag esd uesd converged #> <chr> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> #> 1 C11 18.1 2 0.000117 0.00233 TRUE 0.104 0.104 TRUE 9.4 Your turn In Example 1, refit dif() with p_adjust = "none". Chapter 10 Linking and equating Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain why two separately calibrated forms are not on the same scale; describe common-item (anchor) and common-person designs; link two calibrations with the mean-sigma and Stocking-Lord methods; check anchor items for parameter drift; run a concurrent calibration with a multiple-group model; carry a cut score from one form to another with IRT true-score equating. Key terms: linking, anchor items, moment linking, characteristic curve linking, parameter drift, test characteristic curve. 10.1 The ideas Every calibration fixes the scale by assuming that the people in it have \(\theta\) with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. If this year’s candidates are stronger than last year’s, a separate calibration of this year’s form will still put them at mean 0, and every item will look harder than it is. To compare forms, or groups, the two calibrations must be put on a common scale. That is linking; when the goal is to make scores on two forms interchangeable, it is called equating (Kolen and Brennan 2014). Because the IRT scale is only determined up to a linear transformation, linking amounts to finding two constants \(A\) and \(B\) such that, for the new form’s parameters, \[\theta^* = A\theta + B, \qquad b^* = A b + B, \qquad a^* = a / A.\] The constants come from information the two calibrations share. In the common design, the non-equivalent groups with anchor test (NEAT) design, the two forms share a set of anchor items. Two families of methods estimate \(A\) and \(B\) from the anchors. Moment methods. Mean-sigma matches the mean and standard deviation of the anchor difficulties: \(A = s_{b,\text{old}} / s_{b,\text{new}}\) and \(B = \bar b_\text{old} - A\,\bar b_\text{new}\). They are simple, but sensitive to a single unusual anchor. Characteristic curve methods. Stocking-Lord (Stocking and Lord 1983) chooses \(A\) and \(B\) to make the anchors’ test characteristic curve (the expected anchor score as a function of \(\theta\)) as similar as possible on the two scales. They use all the parameters at once and are more robust. An alternative to linking two separate calibrations is concurrent calibration: Fit one multiple-group model to both forms, constraining the anchor items to be equal across groups and estimating the new group’s mean and standard deviation. Everything rests on the anchors behaving the same way in both administrations. An anchor whose parameters have changed, because it was exposed, taught to, or its position or wording changed, shows parameter drift, and it must be removed from the anchor set before linking. 10.2 Example 1: Separate calibration and linking A language school has an old and a new 30-item placement test that share 10 anchor items. We simulate 1,000 students on each. The new cohort is stronger (mean 0.4, standard deviation 1.1), and anchor A06 was leaked and became easier on the new form. # Simulated NEAT design: old form (O01-O20 + anchors A01-A10) and new form # (N01-N20 + the same anchors); anchor A06 drifts on the new form. set.seed(1010) anchors <- sprintf("A%02d", 1:10) pars <- data.frame(item = c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), anchors), a = rlnorm(50, 0.15, 0.25), b = rnorm(50, 0, 1)) gen <- function(items, n, mean, sd, shift = NULL) { p <- pars[match(items, pars$item), ] if (!is.null(shift)) p$b[p$item %in% names(shift)] <- p$b[p$item %in% names(shift)] + shift out <- simdata(matrix(p$a), matrix(-p$a * p$b), N = n, itemtype = "2PL", Theta = matrix(rnorm(n, mean, sd))) colnames(out) <- items as.data.frame(out) } old <- gen(c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), anchors), 1000, 0, 1) new <- gen(c(sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), anchors), 1000, 0.4, 1.1, shift = c(A06 = -1.2)) Calibrate each form on its own: fit_old <- mirt(old, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) fit_new <- mirt(new, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) p_old <- coef(fit_old, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[anchors, c("a", "b")] p_new <- coef(fit_new, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[anchors, c("a", "b")] round(cbind(b_old = p_old[, "b"], b_new = p_new[, "b"]), 2) #> b_old b_new #> A01 -0.49 -0.90 #> A02 0.69 0.18 #> A03 -1.44 -1.74 #> A04 -0.13 -0.38 #> A05 -1.05 -1.53 #> A06 -0.43 -2.10 #> A07 -1.10 -1.51 #> A08 -0.62 -1.02 #> A09 1.14 0.65 #> A10 -1.82 -2.15 The anchors look easier on the new calibration, because the new students are stronger and their calibration puts them at mean 0. Before linking, check for drift. On a common scale the anchor difficulties should lie on a straight line: library(ggplot2) ggplot(data.frame(old = p_old[, "b"], new = p_new[, "b"], item = anchors), aes(new, old)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey70", formula = y ~ x) + geom_point() + geom_text(aes(label = item), nudge_y = 0.15, size = 3) + labs(x = "Difficulty, new calibration", y = "Difficulty, old calibration") + theme_mirtverse() Figure 10.1: Anchor difficulties in the old and new calibrations; items off the line may have drifted. A06 sits well off the line formed by the others. A simple rule is to flag anchors whose difference in difficulty is far from the typical difference: diff_b <- p_old[, "b"] - p_new[, "b"] round(sort((diff_b - median(diff_b)) / mad(diff_b)), 1) #> A04 A03 A10 A08 A01 A07 A09 A05 A02 A06 #> -1.3 -0.9 -0.7 -0.1 0.0 0.0 0.7 0.7 0.9 10.8 We drop A06 from the anchor set and compute the mean-sigma constants from the remaining nine: keep <- setdiff(anchors, "A06") A <- sd(p_old[keep, "b"]) / sd(p_new[keep, "b"]) B <- mean(p_old[keep, "b"]) - A * mean(p_new[keep, "b"]) c(A = A, B = B) #> A B #> 1.04 0.44 \(B\) estimates how much stronger the new cohort is on the old scale (we simulated 0.4), and \(A\) how much more spread out (1.1). Stocking-Lord finds the constants that make the two anchor characteristic curves agree: tcc <- function(a, b, theta) sapply(theta, function(t) sum(plogis(a * (t - b)))) grid <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 41) sl_loss <- function(k) { A <- k[1]; B <- k[2] sum((tcc(p_old[keep, "a"], p_old[keep, "b"], grid) - tcc(p_new[keep, "a"] / A, A * p_new[keep, "b"] + B, grid))^2 * dnorm(grid)) } sl <- optim(c(1, 0), sl_loss)$par c(A = sl[1], B = sl[2]) #> A B #> 1.05 0.41 Both methods recover the cohort difference well. What would have happened if we had kept the drifted anchor? A_all <- sd(p_old[, "b"]) / sd(p_new[, "b"]) c(A = A_all, B = mean(p_old[, "b"]) - A_all * mean(p_new[, "b"])) #> A B #> 0.963 0.487 One leaked item is enough to distort the link, and with it every score on the new form. 10.3 Example 2: Concurrent calibration and equating a pass mark Concurrent calibration fits both forms at once. We stack the two datasets; each student has NA for the items they did not take. # The same NEAT data stacked: NA for items not on a student's form. # A06 is renamed on the new form, so it is not treated as an anchor. new_a <- new; names(new_a)[names(new_a) == "A06"] <- "A06_new" resp <- merge(transform(old, form = "old", id = seq_len(nrow(old))), transform(new_a, form = "new", id = nrow(old) + seq_len(nrow(new_a))), all = TRUE) form <- factor(resp$form, levels = c("old", "new")) resp <- resp[, setdiff(names(resp), c("form", "id"))] Renaming A06 on the new form turns it into two separate items, one per form, which is the usual way to drop a drifted anchor from the link without discarding its responses. multipleGroup() constrains every item to have the same parameters in both groups (each unique item is only seen by one group anyway) and frees the new group’s mean and variance: mg <- suppressWarnings( multipleGroup(resp, 1, group = form, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE, invariance = c(colnames(resp), "free_means", "free_var"))) coef(mg, simplify = TRUE)$new[c("means", "cov")] #> $means #> F1 #> 0.411 #> #> $cov #> F1 #> F1 1.12 The new group’s mean and variance are estimated on the old group’s scale, and are close to the values we simulated (0.4 and \(1.1^2 = 1.21\)). Now the pass mark. The old form’s pass mark was 18 correct out of 30. What score on the new form corresponds to the same ability? IRT true-score equating finds the \(\theta\) at which the old form’s expected score (its test characteristic curve) equals 18, then reads off the new form’s expected score at that \(\theta\). items <- coef(mg, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$old$items old_items <- c(sprintf("O%02d", 1:20), anchors) new_items <- c(sprintf("N%02d", 1:20), setdiff(anchors, "A06"), "A06_new") tcc_form <- function(ids, theta) tcc(items[ids, "a"], items[ids, "b"], theta) theta_cut <- uniroot(function(t) tcc_form(old_items, t) - 18, c(-4, 4))$root c(theta_cut = theta_cut, new_form_cut = tcc_form(new_items, theta_cut)) #> theta_cut new_form_cut #> 0.419 19.763 curves <- data.frame(theta = rep(grid, 2), score = c(tcc_form(old_items, grid), tcc_form(new_items, grid)), form = rep(c("Old form", "New form"), each = length(grid))) ggplot(curves, aes(theta, score, colour = form)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = theta_cut, linetype = 2) + geom_hline(yintercept = 18, linetype = 3) + labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Expected number correct", colour = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 10.2: Test characteristic curves of the old and new forms on the common scale, with the cut score. If the new form is easier, its curve lies above the old form’s and the pass mark on the new form is higher; if it is harder, the pass mark is lower. Here the new form is a little easier, so the old pass mark of 18 corresponds to about 19.8 on the new form. Rounding the equated score to a whole number is a policy decision: Rounding down passes slightly more candidates than the old standard, rounding up slightly fewer. 10.4 Your turn Repeat the mean-sigma link in Example 1 with the mean-mean method: \(A = \bar a_\text{new} / \bar a_\text{old}\), \(B = \bar b_\text{old} - A\,\bar b_\text{new}\). How close are the constants to the Stocking-Lord ones? Rerun the concurrent calibration of Example 2 with A06 as an anchor. How much does the estimated mean of the new group change? Compute the pass mark on the new form if the old pass mark were 22. A board member asks why the pass mark changed from one year to the next “when the standard was supposed to stay the same”. Answer in two sentences. Solutions A_mm <- mean(p_new[keep, "a"]) / mean(p_old[keep, "a"]) c(A = A_mm, B = mean(p_old[keep, "b"]) - A_mm * mean(p_new[keep, "b"])) #> A B #> 1.025 0.422 resp_all <- merge(transform(old, form = "old", id = seq_len(nrow(old))), transform(new, form = "new", id = nrow(old) + seq_len(nrow(new))), all = TRUE) form_all <- factor(resp_all$form, levels = c("old", "new")) resp_all <- resp_all[, setdiff(names(resp_all), c("form", "id"))] mg_all <- suppressWarnings( multipleGroup(resp_all, 1, group = form_all, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE, invariance = c(colnames(resp_all), "free_means", "free_var"))) coef(mg_all, simplify = TRUE)$new$means #> F1 #> 0.54 theta22 <- uniroot(function(t) tcc_form(old_items, t) - 22, c(-4, 4))$root tcc_form(new_items, theta22) #> [1] 23.1 With A06 treated as an anchor, the new group’s mean rises well above the simulated 0.4. The model has to explain why the new students do so much better on A06; since A06 is constrained to be the same item, part of the leak is credited to the students’ ability. Every new-form score would be too high. For example: “The standard is the same level of ability, not the same number of questions. This year’s form was a little easier, so reaching that level of ability takes a slightly higher number of correct answers.” In the lab Lab 4, run_lab("linking"), asks why a licensure exam’s pass rate jumped on a new form. You calibrate both forms, link them, check the anchors, compare separate and concurrent calibration, and carry the pass mark over. Chapter 11 Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe what an item bank stores and what it is for; read a bank’s information curve and spot where the bank is thin; assemble a fixed form from a bank under content constraints; explain, step by step, how a computerized adaptive test (CAT) selects items, scores people and decides when to stop; judge a CAT design by its precision, test length and item exposure. Key terms: item bank, automated test assembly, parallel forms, computerized adaptive test, multistage test, exposure. 11.1 The ideas Once items have been calibrated on a common scale (Chapter 10), their parameters can be stored in an item bank together with their content codes, usage history and review status. Because the parameters are on one scale, any selection of items from the bank yields scores on that scale. That makes two things possible. Automated test assembly (ATA) picks items for a fixed form so that the form meets a blueprint (for example, ten items from each content area) and its information curve matches a target: High at a cut score for a licensing test, flat across the range for a progress test (Linden 2005). Exact solutions use mixed-integer programming; simple greedy rules, which add the best remaining item that still fits the blueprint, often get close. A computerized adaptive test (CAT) goes further and builds a different test for every person while they take it (Wainer et al. 2000). The loop is: Start with a provisional \(\theta\) (often 0). Choose the unused item with the most information at the current \(\theta\), subject to content and exposure rules. Score the response and update \(\theta\) (usually by EAP, which works even after one item). Stop when the standard error is small enough or a maximum length is reached; otherwise go back to step 2. A CAT typically reaches the precision of a fixed test with half as many items or fewer. The price is a bank large enough to cover the whole range, and exposure: Without control, the most informative items are given to almost everybody and soon become known. A multistage test (MST) is a compromise: People take pre-assembled modules, and the next module depends on their performance on the last one. 11.2 Example 1: A vocabulary bank and a fixed form A language-assessment centre has a calibrated bank of 200 vocabulary items in four areas. # A calibrated 2PL item bank: 200 items, four content areas. set.seed(1111) bank <- data.frame(item = sprintf("V%03d", 1:200), area = factor(rep(c("Everyday", "Academic", "Workplace", "Idioms"), each = 50)), a = rlnorm(200, 0.2, 0.3), b = c(rnorm(50, -0.8, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0.4, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0.9, 0.7))) The bank’s information curve, overall and by area, shows where it can measure well: item_info <- function(a, b, theta) { p <- plogis(a * (theta - b)); a^2 * p * (1 - p) } grid <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1) bank_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(bank$area), function(ar) { s <- bank[bank$area == ar, ] data.frame(area = ar, theta = grid, info = sapply(grid, function(t) sum(item_info(s$a, s$b, t)))) })) library(ggplot2) ggplot(bank_info, aes(theta, info, fill = area)) + geom_area() + labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Bank information", fill = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 11.1: Information of the 200-item vocabulary bank, stacked by content area. The bank is rich in the middle and thin at the extremes, especially below \(\theta = -2\) and above \(\theta = 2\). Everyday vocabulary covers the low end, idioms the high end. Item writers should be asked for very easy and very hard items. Now a 24-item fixed form with six items from each area, to measure well between \(\theta = -1\) and \(\theta = 1\). A greedy assembly adds, one at a time, the item that adds the most information at the target points, as long as its area is not yet full: assemble_greedy <- function(bank, length, per_area, targets) { chosen <- integer(0) while (length(chosen) < length) { full <- names(which(table(bank$area[chosen]) >= per_area)) cand <- setdiff(which(!bank$area %in% full), chosen) gain <- sapply(cand, function(i) sum(item_info(bank$a[i], bank$b[i], targets))) chosen <- c(chosen, cand[which.max(gain)]) } bank[chosen, ] } form <- assemble_greedy(bank, length = 24, per_area = 6, targets = c(-1, 0, 1)) table(form$area) #> #> Academic Everyday Idioms Workplace #> 6 6 6 6 Compared with a random 24-item form that meets the same blueprint: random_form <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(bank, bank$area), function(s) s[sample(50, 6), ])) se_at <- function(f, theta) 1 / sqrt(sapply(theta, function(t) sum(item_info(f$a, f$b, t)))) round(rbind(assembled = se_at(form, c(-1, 0, 1)), random = se_at(random_form, c(-1, 0, 1))), 3) #> [,1] [,2] [,3] #> assembled 0.265 0.236 0.276 #> random 0.318 0.304 0.332 The assembled form measures more precisely at all three target points with the same length and blueprint. For real programmes, assemble_forms() in the mirtverse assessment pipeline solves the same problem exactly, builds several parallel forms at once and handles enemy items (items that must not appear together). 11.3 Example 2: A CAT from scratch We now write a complete CAT in about 30 lines, using the same bank. The scoring step computes the EAP estimate on a grid of quadrature points, with a standard normal prior. quad <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 81) prior <- dnorm(quad) eap <- function(a, b, x) { like <- sapply(quad, function(t) prod(ifelse(x == 1, plogis(a * (t - b)), 1 - plogis(a * (t - b))))) post <- like * prior / sum(like * prior) est <- sum(quad * post) c(theta = est, se = sqrt(sum((quad - est)^2 * post))) } cat_one <- function(true_theta, bank, se_stop = 0.3, max_items = 30, top = 1) { used <- integer(0); x <- integer(0); est <- c(theta = 0, se = 1) while (length(used) < max_items && est["se"] > se_stop) { info <- item_info(bank$a, bank$b, est["theta"]); info[used] <- -Inf best <- order(info, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(top)] item <- if (top == 1) best else sample(best, 1) # randomesque exposure control used <- c(used, item) x <- c(x, rbinom(1, 1, plogis(bank$a[item] * (true_theta - bank$b[item])))) est <- eap(bank$a[used], bank$b[used], x) } list(theta = est[["theta"]], se = est[["se"]], n = length(used), items = used) } Simulate 300 test takers across the ability range. (To run the CAT on your own bank, replace bank in the data chunk of Example 1; it needs columns item, area, a and b.) # Simulated test takers for the CAT: one true theta per person. set.seed(1112) true_theta <- rnorm(300) runs <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank) res <- data.frame(true = true_theta, est = sapply(runs, `[[`, "theta"), se = sapply(runs, `[[`, "se"), n = sapply(runs, `[[`, "n")) c(mean_length = mean(res$n), rmse = sqrt(mean((res$est - res$true)^2)), cor = cor(res$est, res$true)) #> mean_length rmse cor #> 12.337 0.292 0.959 On average the CAT reaches a standard error of 0.3 with far fewer than 30 items. Test length depends on where a person is: In the middle, where the bank is rich, the CAT stops quickly; at the extremes it runs out of informative items and goes to the maximum. ggplot(res, aes(true, n)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + labs(x = "True theta", y = "Items administered") + theme_mirtverse() Figure 11.2: Number of items administered by the CAT against true ability. Exposure is the other side of the coin. With pure maximum-information selection, a few items are given to a large share of test takers: exposure <- function(runs) { table(factor(unlist(lapply(runs, `[[`, "items")), levels = 1:200)) / length(runs) } exp_max <- exposure(runs) sort(round(exp_max, 2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:6] #> #> 31 100 97 67 135 140 #> 1.00 0.68 0.64 0.60 0.48 0.48 The first item is the same for everybody (the most informative item at \(\theta = 0\)), so its exposure is 100%. The randomesque method picks at random among the five most informative items, which spreads exposure at a small cost in test length: set.seed(1113) runs_r <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank, top = 5) exp_r <- exposure(runs_r) rbind(max_info = c(max_exposure = max(exp_max), mean_length = mean(sapply(runs, `[[`, "n"))), randomesque = c(max_exposure = max(exp_r), mean_length = mean(sapply(runs_r, `[[`, "n")))) #> max_exposure mean_length #> max_info 1.000 12.3 #> randomesque 0.677 12.9 Content balancing (for example, cycling through the four areas) works the same way: Restrict the candidate items before choosing the most informative one. simulate_cat() in the assessment pipeline runs this kind of simulation on a real bank, and the mirtCAT package can deliver an operational CAT. 11.4 Your turn Add 20 hard items (\(b \sim N(2.2, 0.4)\)) to the bank in Example 1 and redraw the information curve. What happens to CAT length for the most able test takers? Change the stopping rule to \(SE < 0.25\). How do mean length and RMSE change? Add content balancing to cat_one() so that each test has at least four items from every area. (Hint: While an area has fewer than four items, restrict the candidates to that area.) An admissions officer asks why two applicants got different questions and different numbers of questions. Write a short explanation. Chapter 12 Cut scores, reporting and communicating results Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe the Bookmark standard-setting method and build an item map at a response probability of 0.67; turn a cut on the \(\theta\) scale into a raw-score cut; estimate classification accuracy and consistency at a cut score; report IRT results to people who do not use R, with a written summary, a report and a dashboard. Key terms: cut score, standard setting, response probability, classification accuracy, classification consistency, test characteristic curve. 12.1 The ideas A cut score divides a scale into categories such as pass and fail, or below basic, proficient and advanced. Where the cut goes is a judgement about what performance is good enough, made by people who know the content and the consequences. Standard setting is the family of structured procedures for making that judgement defensibly (Cizek and Bunch 2007). The Bookmark method is closely tied to IRT. Items are ordered from easiest to hardest in an ordered item booklet, where each item’s location is the \(\theta\) at which a test taker has a fixed probability (usually 0.67, the response probability RP67) of answering it correctly. Each panelist places a bookmark after the last item that a just-qualified candidate should master. The location of the bookmarked item is that panelist’s cut, and the panel’s cut is usually the median over panelists after several rounds of discussion. For a 2PL item, the RP67 location is \[\theta_{0.67} = b + \frac{\ln(0.67/0.33)}{a}.\] Once a cut is fixed on the \(\theta\) scale, two numbers describe how well the test sorts people. Classification accuracy is the proportion of people whose estimated category matches their true category. Classification consistency is the proportion who would be placed in the same category on two independent administrations of the test. Both can be estimated from a single administration using the scores and their standard errors (Rudner 2001). Finally, results have to be communicated. People who make decisions with test scores rarely read item parameters. They need a short, honest summary of what the test measures, how precisely, for whom it works, and what the scores mean. 12.2 Example 1: Setting a proficiency standard A provincial Grade 6 science test has 36 items. We simulate a calibration on 2,500 students. # Simulated 36-item science test, 2,500 students. set.seed(1212) a <- matrix(rlnorm(36, 0.15, 0.25)); b <- sort(rnorm(36, 0, 1)) resp <- simdata(a, matrix(-a * b), N = 2500, itemtype = "2PL") colnames(resp) <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:36) mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) pars <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items booklet <- data.frame(item = rownames(pars), a = pars[, "a"], b = pars[, "b"]) booklet$rp67 <- booklet$b + log(0.67 / 0.33) / booklet$a booklet <- booklet[order(booklet$rp67), ] booklet$page <- seq_len(nrow(booklet)) head(booklet, 8) #> item a b rp67 page #> S02 S02 1.924 -1.473 -1.105 1 #> S01 S01 0.928 -1.827 -1.064 2 #> S03 S03 1.243 -1.387 -0.818 3 #> S05 S05 1.335 -0.955 -0.425 4 #> S06 S06 1.118 -1.011 -0.377 5 #> S04 S04 0.833 -1.090 -0.239 6 #> S08 S08 1.245 -0.741 -0.173 7 #> S10 S10 1.931 -0.488 -0.121 8 The ordered item booklet is booklet, one page per item. Suppose eight panelists, after two rounds of discussion, place their bookmarks for proficient on these pages: bookmarks <- c(20, 22, 21, 23, 22, 24, 21, 22) panel_cuts <- booklet$rp67[bookmarks] theta_cut <- median(panel_cuts) c(theta_cut = theta_cut, spread = sd(panel_cuts)) #> theta_cut spread #> 0.7943 0.0586 The standard deviation of the panelists’ cuts, divided by the square root of the number of panelists, is a rough standard error of the panel’s cut. It should be reported alongside the cut. Teachers and parents see raw scores, so we convert the cut with the test characteristic curve: The expected number correct at \(\theta\). raw_cut <- expected.test(mod, matrix(theta_cut)) c(theta_cut = theta_cut, expected_raw = raw_cut, raw_cut = ceiling(raw_cut)) #> theta_cut expected_raw raw_cut #> 0.794 24.583 25.000 How many students are classified as proficient, and how accurately? sc <- fscores(mod, full.scores.SE = TRUE) above <- sc[, 1] >= theta_cut p_above <- pnorm((sc[, 1] - theta_cut) / sc[, 2]) c(percent_proficient = mean(above), accuracy = mean(ifelse(above, p_above, 1 - p_above)), consistency = mean(p_above^2 + (1 - p_above)^2)) #> percent_proficient accuracy consistency #> 0.204 0.925 0.893 Accuracy compares each student’s category with where their true score probably lies; consistency asks how often two independent testings would agree (here approximated from each student’s posterior probability of being above the cut). Consistency is always the lower of the two, because both testings carry error. An item map makes the cut concrete for teachers: It shows which items a just-proficient student is likely to answer correctly (the items below the line). Printing the text of a few items on each side of the line is a good way to describe what proficient means. library(ggplot2) ggplot(booklet, aes(page, rp67, colour = rp67 <= theta_cut)) + geom_hline(yintercept = theta_cut, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2) + annotate("text", x = 1, y = theta_cut + 0.15, label = "Proficient cut", colour = "#C0392B", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#2C5F8A", `FALSE` = "grey60"), labels = c(`TRUE` = "mastered at the cut", `FALSE` = "not yet")) + labs(x = "Page in the ordered item booklet", y = "RP67 location (theta)", colour = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 12.1: Item map of the ordered item booklet with the proficient cut score. In a real programme, item_map() and set_cuts() in the assessment pipeline produce the booklet, record the panel’s judgements, and report impact and classification statistics for several cuts at once. 12.3 Example 2: Telling the story We return to the attitude scale from Chapter 8 to show the reporting tools on a different kind of instrument. # Four 4-category attitude items (scored 1-4), 392 respondents. resp <- Science select_model() and interpret() give a plain-language summary that is a good first draft for the methods and results sections of a report: sel <- select_model(resp, verbose = FALSE) interpret(sel$best) #> Overview #> -------- #> * A graded model with 1 dimension was fitted to 392 respondents and 4 items #> (EM estimation). #> * The estimation converged normally. #> #> Model fit #> --------- #> * Overall model fit is poor: C2 = 19.18, df = 2, RMSEA = 0.148, CFI = 0.910, #> SRMSR = 0.073. #> #> Reliability #> ----------- #> * Marginal reliability is 0.67 (low). #> * Scores are too imprecise for decisions about individuals; consider adding #> items or using the scores only for group-level summaries. #> #> Targeting #> --------- #> * The average item location is -0.99 and the average person score is 0.00, so #> the test is relatively easy for this group. #> * Measurement is most precise around theta = -2.20 (information = 2.42, SE = #> 0.64). #> #> Items #> ----- #> * No items were flagged for low discrimination, extreme location, or misfit. #> #> Local dependence #> ---------------- #> * 1 item pair shows possible local dependence (Q3 exceeds the average of #> -0.19 by more than 0.2). #> * Strongest: Comfort & Benefit (Q3 = 0.08). #> * Check whether these items share a stimulus, wording, or content; consider a #> testlet or bifactor model. #> #> Person fit #> ---------- #> * 4.8% of respondents have unusual response patterns (Zh < -1.96), which is #> within what chance alone would produce. Read it critically before you use it: It flags the poor absolute fit and the low precision, and a careful report says what that means for the intended use of the scores. interpret_prompt() packages the same results into a prompt you can paste into an AI assistant to draft a longer narrative. Nothing is sent anywhere. For people who want to see everything, mirtverse writes a complete HTML report in one call, with the model comparison, the interpretation, tables, figures, a sum-score conversion table, item health cards and the code to reproduce it: mv_report(sel, file = "science-attitudes-report.html") For people who want to explore, a dashboard lets them move an ability slider, click through items and download tables, without R: mv_dashboard(sel$best, title = "Attitudes to science") export_dashboard(sel$best, "science-dashboard.html", format = "html") See Sharing results with a dashboard for the options. 12.3.1 A one-page memo Decision makers usually want one page. A structure that works: The question. What decision will the scores support? The answer. One or two sentences: Can the test support it? The evidence. Three to five bullets: Precision where the decision is made, classification accuracy, fairness checks, any items removed. What it means. The consequences of the cut for the people tested, for example the percentage classified in each category and how many are close to the cut. Recommendations and limits. 12.4 Your turn In Example 1, how many raw-score points does the cut move if every panelist moves their bookmark one page later? Repeat the item map with RP50 instead of RP67. Does the cut move up or down? Why does the choice of response probability matter to panelists? Add a second cut for advanced at page 30. Estimate the accuracy of the three-category classification. Write the “answer” and “evidence” parts of a memo about the proficiency cut in Example 1. Solutions cut_later <- median(booklet$rp67[bookmarks + 1]) c(expected.test(mod, matrix(theta_cut)), expected.test(mod, matrix(cut_later))) #> [1] 24.6 24.7 rp50 <- sort(booklet$b) c(rp67_cut = theta_cut, rp50_cut = median(rp50[bookmarks])) #> rp67_cut rp50_cut #> 0.794 0.100 adv <- median(booklet$rp67[rep(30, 8)]) cats <- cut(sc[, 1], c(-Inf, theta_cut, adv, Inf), labels = c("below", "proficient", "advanced")) p_cat <- cbind(pnorm((theta_cut - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]), pnorm((adv - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]) - pnorm((theta_cut - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2]), 1 - pnorm((adv - sc[, 1]) / sc[, 2])) mean(p_cat[cbind(seq_len(nrow(p_cat)), as.integer(cats))]) #> [1] 0.88 Hardly at all here, because the items in that part of the booklet have very similar RP67 locations. Where the booklet has gaps between items, a single page can move the cut a lot, which is worth showing panelists. With RP50 every item’s location is lower, so the same bookmark gives a lower cut. Panelists must understand what “mastered” means (a 50% or a 67% chance), or their bookmarks will not mean what they intend. For example: “The test can support a proficient/not proficient decision. About 93% of students are expected to be classified correctly, and 89% would be classified the same way if tested again. The panel’s eight judgements were close together, and about one student in five is classified as proficient.” Use the numbers from your own output, and add the standard error at the cut (1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, matrix(theta_cut)))). Chapter 13 Machine learning through an IRT lens Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain the difference between a prediction model and a measurement model, and say what each can and cannot claim; show that a 2PL item response function is a logistic regression on a latent predictor, and what goes wrong when an observed score stands in for it; estimate how well a model predicts new cases with cross-validation, and recognize overfitting; explain why a single IRT score often predicts better than all the item responses fed to a flexible model. Key terms: machine learning, feature, overfitting and cross-validation, latent trait. The translation table pairs many more machine learning words with their psychometric relatives. 13.1 The ideas Machine learning (ML) is a set of methods for learning a rule that predicts an outcome from data. It is judged by one question: How well does the rule predict cases it has not seen? Breiman (2001) called this the algorithmic culture of statistics, in contrast to the data modelling culture that psychometrics grew up in, where a model is a claim about how the data arose and its parameters mean something. An IRT model makes such a claim. The 2PL says that the chance of a correct answer depends on one unobserved trait through a logistic curve whose slope and location are properties of the item. That is a logistic regression, with one twist: The predictor \(\theta\) is never observed. Everything that makes IRT useful follows from taking that claim seriously: Item parameters that do not depend on who took the test, a standard error for every score, information to design tests with, and checks of fit that can reject the model. A prediction model makes a weaker promise. It does not say why the outcome happens, only that its rule will predict well in data like the training data. In exchange it can use any predictors (features) in any flexible form. Two habits of ML are worth taking home even if you never fit a neural network: Hold data out. A model always fits the data it was estimated on better than new data, and a flexible model can fit noise. This is overfitting, and the cure is to judge a model on data it did not see. Cross-validation splits the data into k parts (folds), fits the model on \(k - 1\) of them, predicts the one left out, and repeats until every case has been predicted once (James et al. 2021). Shrink. Penalizing large coefficients (ridge, lasso) trades a little bias for a large cut in variance. It is the same idea as a prior on item parameters, or as MAP and EAP scoring pulling extreme scores toward the mean. Yarkoni and Westfall (2017) make the case that psychology should care more about prediction. The examples below show the reverse lesson as well: A good measurement model is itself a very effective way to predict. 13.2 Example 1: The 2PL is a logistic regression on theta We simulate 20 items answered by 2,000 test takers whose true abilities we keep, so we can do something impossible with real data: Regress each item on the true \(\theta\). # Simulated 20-item test with known abilities and item parameters. set.seed(1313) n <- 2000 theta <- rnorm(n) a <- round(rlnorm(20, log(1.3), 0.3), 2) b <- round(sort(rnorm(20, 0, 1)), 2) p <- plogis(outer(theta, a) - matrix(a * b, n, 20, byrow = TRUE)) resp <- as.data.frame((matrix(runif(n * 20), n) < p) * 1L) names(resp) <- sprintf("Q%02d", 1:20) A logistic regression of item 5 on the true \(\theta\) estimates its slope and intercept directly; on the logit scale the intercept is \(-ab\): fit5 <- glm(resp$Q05 ~ theta, family = binomial) c(slope = unname(coef(fit5)[2]), b = unname(-coef(fit5)[1] / coef(fit5)[2]), true_a = a[5], true_b = b[5]) #> slope b true_a true_b #> 1.328 -0.139 1.210 -0.190 With real data we do not have \(\theta\). The obvious stand-in is the sum score. Doing the same regression on the standardized rest score (the sum of the other 19 items) gives slopes that are on average about a fifth too flat, because the rest score measures \(\theta\) with error (Figure 13.1). IRT avoids this by estimating \(\theta\) and the item parameters together: mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) est <- coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items slope_obs <- sapply(1:20, function(j) { rest <- scale(rowSums(resp[, -j])) coef(glm(resp[[j]] ~ rest, family = binomial))[2] }) round(c(true = mean(a), irt = mean(est[, "a"]), rest_score = mean(slope_obs)), 2) #> true irt rest_score #> 1.28 1.26 1.05 slopes <- rbind(data.frame(true = a, estimate = est[, "a"], method = "2PL (mirt)"), data.frame(true = a, estimate = slope_obs, method = "Regression on rest score")) ggplot2::ggplot(slopes, ggplot2::aes(true, estimate, colour = method)) + ggplot2::geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) + ggplot2::labs(x = "True slope (a)", y = "Estimated slope", colour = NULL) + theme_mirtverse() Figure 13.1: Item slopes estimated by the 2PL and by logistic regression on the standardized rest score, against the true slopes. The dashed line marks perfect recovery. The lesson carries over to every ML model that uses test scores as features: An observed score is a noisy measure of the trait, and models that ignore the noise underestimate how strongly the trait relates to anything else. 13.3 Example 2: Forty items or one score? A university wants to predict which applicants will pass a first-year statistics course from a 40-item placement test. We simulate 400 past students whose course result depends only on their ability, plus noise. # Simulated 40-item placement test and a pass/fail course outcome. set.seed(2027) n <- 400 ability <- rnorm(n) a2 <- rlnorm(40, log(1.1), 0.3) b2 <- rnorm(40, 0, 1) p2 <- plogis(outer(ability, a2) - matrix(a2 * b2, n, 40, byrow = TRUE)) resp <- as.data.frame((matrix(runif(n * 40), n) < p2) * 1L) names(resp) <- sprintf("P%02d", 1:40) passed <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.6 * ability + 0.3)) The ML approach feeds all 40 item responses to a classifier as features. The measurement approach first summarizes them in one IRT score and uses only that. Both are logistic regressions here, so the comparison is about the features, not the algorithm. We judge each by its accuracy on the data it was fitted to and with 10-fold cross-validation: theta_hat <- fscores(mirt(resp, 1, verbose = FALSE))[, 1] dat <- data.frame(passed, theta_hat, resp) accuracy <- function(fit, newdata) mean((predict(fit, newdata, type = "response") > 0.5) == newdata$passed) cv <- function(formula, k = 10) { fold <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(dat))) mean(sapply(1:k, function(f) { fit <- suppressWarnings(glm(formula, binomial, data = dat[fold != f, ])) accuracy(fit, dat[fold == f, ]) })) } items_formula <- reformulate(names(resp), "passed") set.seed(1) data.frame( features = c("40 item responses", "one IRT score"), training_accuracy = c(accuracy(suppressWarnings(glm(items_formula, binomial, data = dat)), dat), accuracy(glm(passed ~ theta_hat, binomial, data = dat), dat)), cv_accuracy = c(cv(items_formula), cv(passed ~ theta_hat))) #> features training_accuracy cv_accuracy #> 1 40 item responses 0.787 0.720 #> 2 one IRT score 0.735 0.742 On the training data the 40-item model looks better: With 41 coefficients it can fit some of the noise. Cross-validation tells the truth. On new students it does worse than the single score, because the IRT model has already done what a good ML pipeline would have had to learn: That the items measure one thing and should be combined with weights close to their discriminations. A measurement model is a strong, theory-based form of regularization. This is not an argument against ML. With thousands of students, features that carry information beyond the trait (response times, the text of answers), or an outcome that depends on more than one trait, a flexible model may well win. The point is to compare on held-out data and to know what each approach is claiming. 13.4 Your turn In Example 1, repeat the rest-score regression using the EAP score from fscores(mod) instead of the rest score. Are the slopes closer to the truth? Why not? In Example 2, change n to 2,000 in the data chunk and run the comparison again. What happens to the gap between the two approaches, and why? Shrinking the 40 item coefficients toward a common value reduces overfitting; giving every item the same weight, the proportion correct rowMeans(resp), is the extreme case. How does a model on the proportion correct do under cross-validation in Example 2? A vendor reports that their ML model “predicts course success with 82% accuracy” from your placement test items. Write three questions you would ask before believing it. Solutions # 1. the same regression on the EAP score of Example 1 resp1 <- extract.mirt(mod, "data") eap <- fscores(mod)[, 1] slope_eap <- sapply(1:20, function(j) coef(glm(resp1[, j] ~ eap, family = binomial))[2]) round(c(true = mean(a), eap = mean(slope_eap)), 2) #> true eap #> 1.28 1.56 # 3. equal weights: the extreme form of shrinkage dat$prop <- rowMeans(resp) set.seed(1) cv(passed ~ prop) #> [1] 0.74 Now the slopes are too steep on average. EAP scores are shrunk toward the mean, so their spread is smaller than \(\theta\)’s and each unit of EAP corresponds to more than one unit of \(\theta\); and each item’s own response helped compute the EAP score it is regressed on. An estimated score is not \(\theta\), whichever way you compute it; that is why IRT estimates the item parameters and the trait distribution together. With 2,000 students the 40-item model has more data per coefficient, so it overfits less and the cross-validated gap narrows. It still rarely beats the IRT score, because the outcome depends only on the trait. The proportion correct does about as well as the IRT score under cross-validation: Equal weights are a strong form of shrinkage and lose little when the items’ discriminations are similar. For example: Was the 82% computed on students who were not used to train the model? What is the accuracy of predicting from the total score alone, or of predicting that everyone passes? Is the accuracy similar for subgroups of students, such as English language learners? Chapter 14 What item text tells us Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain why predicting item difficulty from text is useful, and what it can and cannot replace; describe items by text features with item_features(), and connect them to the item covariates of the linear logistic test model (LLTM); predict difficulty with an explanatory model, a lasso and a random forest using predict_difficulty(), and compare them by cross-validation; fit the one-step LLTM to responses in mirt; recognize leakage, choose the right unit to hold out, and know the limit set by the error in estimated difficulties. Key terms: Feature, LLTM, overfitting and cross-validation, embedding, data leakage. 14.1 The ideas Every new item needs a difficulty before it can be used for scoring, and the usual way to get one is a field test: The item is given to hundreds of test takers and calibrated (Chapter 3). Field testing is slow and expensive, and it exposes items before they count. Item writers also know that some features make items harder: More reading, an extra step, a negation, decimals instead of whole numbers. If difficulty could be predicted from the text, a program could target field-test forms, use smaller field-test samples, steer item writing towards the difficulties the bank lacks, and judge items written by a generator (Chapter 17). Psychometrics and machine learning both have a way of doing this. Explanatory IRT. The linear logistic test model (Fischer 1973) replaces each item’s difficulty with a weighted sum of its features: \[b_i = \eta_0 + \sum_k \eta_k q_{ik},\] where \(q_{ik}\) is the value of feature \(k\) for item \(i\) (the item’s covariates) and \(\eta_k\) is how much the feature adds to difficulty, in logits. The weights are read as evidence about what makes items hard, which is a claim about the construct (De Boeck and Wilson 2004). The model can be fitted to the responses in one step, or in two steps by regressing estimated difficulties on the features. Prediction. Machine learning treats difficulty as a label to predict from as many features as are useful: Counts and readability measures, word frequencies, or embeddings of the text from a language model. Models such as the lasso or a random forest are judged by how well they predict items they were not trained on (AlKhuzaey et al. 2024; Benedetto et al. 2023). The two are less different than they look. The two-step LLTM is a linear regression, and the lasso is the same regression with its weights shrunk. What differs is the goal: Explaining difficulty, or predicting it as accurately as possible. Three cautions apply to both. Leakage. A feature computed from the same responses as the difficulty, such as the proportion correct in the field test, predicts difficulty almost perfectly and is useless, because it is not available until the item has been field-tested. What is held out. Items written from the same template (an item model) share most of their difficulty. A model that has seen other items from an item’s template predicts it well; a model asked about a new kind of item usually does much worse. Cross-validation must hold out the unit you will predict for. The noise floor. Estimated difficulties have standard errors, and features never capture everything that makes an item hard. No model can predict \(b\) more closely than its estimation error, and an LLTM rarely fits as well as giving every item its own difficulty. Real benchmarks show modest gains over simple baselines (Yaneva et al. 2024). 14.2 Example 1: Features and an explanatory model A science program has 70 multiple-choice items of the form “Which of these is a mammal?”, on seven topics. Half the items are negated (“Which of these is NOT a mammal?”), half start with a context sentence that adds reading but no content, and in some the key happens to be the longest option, a cue that test-wise students use. On items they have not seen, the two linear models explain a little under 60% of the variance in difficulty (\(R^2\)), with a typical error (RMSE) of about 0.4 logits. The random forest does worse: With 70 items and effects that simply add up, its flexibility buys nothing. The LLTM’s weights say what the features do: tidy(m1)[tidy(m1)$method == "lltm", ] #> # A tibble: 5 × 4 #> method term estimate std_error #> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 lltm (Intercept) -0.835 0.171 #> 2 lltm sentences 0.181 0.0968 #> 3 lltm negation 0.670 0.100 #> 4 lltm option_words 0.478 0.0619 #> 5 lltm key_longest -0.292 0.128 A negation adds about two thirds of a logit, a context sentence about 0.2, and a longest key makes an item easier, as item writers would expect. option_words has a large weight too, which is less plausible as a cause: Long options belong to the harder topics, such as physical changes. The features know nothing about topic, so they stand in for it where they can. Adding the topic as a feature brings the error down to about 0.29 logits (Exercise 1), close to the 0.25 of item-specific variation built into the simulation, and the weight of option_words shrinks to almost nothing. 14.3 Example 2: The one-step LLTM in mirt The two-step LLTM treats the estimated difficulties as known. The one-step LLTM fits the features to the responses directly: Each item’s difficulty is constrained to the weighted sum of its features. In mirt, the features are passed as itemdesign and the model for them as item.formula. Here each topic gets its own intercept: design <- data.frame(topic = factor(sci$topic), feats[, c("sentences", "negation", "key_longest")]) lltm <- mirt(as.data.frame(resp), 1, "Rasch", itemdesign = design, item.formula = ~ 0 + topic + sentences + negation + key_longest, verbose = FALSE) v <- mod2values(lltm) eta <- v[v$item == sci$id[1] & v$name %in% c("sentences", "negation", "key_longest"), c("name", "value")] eta$difficulty <- -eta$value # mirt models easiness; reverse the sign for difficulty eta #> name value difficulty #> 8 sentences -0.21 0.21 #> 9 negation -0.62 0.62 #> 10 key_longest 0.32 -0.32 A context sentence adds about 0.2 logits, a negation about 0.6, and a longest key makes an item about 0.3 logits easier: Close to the two-step weights and to the values used to simulate the data. The classic test of an LLTM compares it with the Rasch model, which gives every item its own difficulty: anova(lltm, rasch) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> lltm 81315 81334 81336 81369 -40647 #> rasch 80664 80787 80797 81013 -40261 770.603 60 0 Ten parameters cannot replace 70 free difficulties, and the likelihood ratio test says so loudly; with 1,000 test takers it nearly always does. The LLTM is still useful: It shows which features matter and by how much. Explanatory IRT models that add a random item effect, so that each item may differ from its features’ prediction, combine the two views (De Boeck and Wilson 2004). They are generalized linear mixed models, and the eirm package (Bulut et al. 2021) fits them with lme4 from data in long format, one row per person and item. The model below keeps the LLTM’s features and adds a random effect for items, whose variance is the difficulty the features leave unexplained (eirm reports easiness, so the signs are reversed again): # install.packages("eirm") library(eirm) long <- data.frame(person = rep(seq_len(nrow(resp)), ncol(resp)), item = rep(colnames(resp), each = nrow(resp)), resp = as.vector(resp)) long <- merge(long, data.frame(item = sci$id, design)) m_eirm <- eirm("resp ~ -1 + topic + sentences + negation + key_longest + (1|person) + (1|item)", data = long) print(m_eirm, difficulty = TRUE) # fixed effects as difficulties lme4::VarCorr(m_eirm$model) # person and residual item variance The same framework adds person covariates, such as language status, and their interactions with item features, which is DIF explained by features rather than item by item. 14.4 Example 3: New items or new kinds of items? So far each fold held out random items, so every topic was in training. A new item on a known topic is one question; a topic the model has never seen is another. Hold out whole topics with group: m3 <- predict_difficulty(items, c("topic", "sentences", "negation", "key_longest"), group = "topic", methods = "lltm") m3$accuracy #> # A tibble: 1 × 5 #> method rmse mae r r2 #> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 lltm 0.592 0.473 0.445 0.153 With its topic held out, an item is predicted as if it belonged to an average topic, and the error doubles to about 0.6 logits; \(R^2\) falls to about 0.15. The features still capture negation, the context sentence and the longest key, but the topic, the largest part of an item’s difficulty, cannot be read off the text. This is the usual finding: Text features place items within a family much better than they predict how hard a new kind of item will be. That is why automatic item generation calibrates item models rather than single items. Chapter 15 Generating items Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain automatic item generation (AIG) from item models, and how it differs from asking a language model for items; write an item model with item_model(), with distractors built from misconceptions and constraints that rule out flawed items, and generate isomorphs with generate_isomorphs(); check after field testing whether a family of isomorphs is equally difficult with calibrate_families(), and find the variable that makes a family spread; fit a one-step model with a random item effect in mirt, or with eirm, and say when a family mean can stand in for a field test. Key terms: Item model, LLTM, calibration. 15.1 The ideas Testing programs need many items: For new forms each year, for adaptive tests that must not expose the same items too often (Chapter 11), and for practice. Writing and field-testing each item by hand is the slowest and most expensive part of test development. Automatic item generation (AIG) writes items from a template (Gierl and Haladyna 2013; Gierl and Lai 2013). An item model is a parent item with variable parts: A stem, a key and distractors, each written as a template, the values each variable can take, and constraints that every generated item must meet. Filling in the values gives isomorphs: Items that test the same thing in the same way and differ only in their surface, such as the numbers. Two promises come with item models. The first is quality at scale: If the model is right, every item it generates is right, and an error in the model shows up in every item, where an automatic check can catch it. The second is calibration at the level of the family. If isomorphs are equally difficult, the item model can be calibrated once, and its new items can use the family’s difficulty without a field test of their own (Glas and van der Linden 2003; Sinharay et al. 2003). That promise is an empirical claim, and this chapter is about checking it. A family’s items are never exactly equally difficult. The model for a family \(f\) is \[b_i = \mu_f + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma_f^2),\] where \(\mu_f\) is the family’s mean difficulty and \(\sigma_f\), the within-family SD, says how much its isomorphs differ. A new item’s difficulty is predicted by \(\mu_f\) with an error of about \(\sigma_f\). When \(\sigma_f\) is small, the family mean is as good as a field test of a few hundred test takers; when it is large, some variable in the item model changes what the items demand, and the model must be split or the variable added as a feature, as in the LLTM of Chapter 14. Explanatory IRT treats this as one model with item features and a random item effect (De Boeck and Wilson 2004; Geerlings et al. 2011). Language models offer a second route: Ask for items in a prompt (generate_items(), Chapter 17). They write more varied items, but each is a one-off, with no template to calibrate and no guarantee that two items with the same prompt are isomorphs. Template-based AIG is predictable and traceable; every item can be rebuilt from its values. In practice the two meet: Language models can help write item models, and their items can be reviewed with the same checks. 15.2 Example 1: Writing an item model An average speed item has two variables, the speed v and the time t. Writing the distance as v * t keeps the answer a whole number. Each distractor is the answer of a misconception: # Item models for a simulated Grade 7 field test. speed <- item_model( stem = "A train travels {v * t} km in {t} hours. What is its average speed?", key = "{v} km/h", distractors = c(multiplied = "{v * t * t} km/h", subtracted = "{v * t - t} km/h", added = "{v * t + t} km/h"), values = list(v = seq(40, 120, 10), t = 2:6), name = "SPD") frac <- item_model( stem = "A class of {n} students voted. {num}/{den} of them chose soccer. How many students chose soccer?", key = "{n * num / den}", distractors = c(multiplied_only = "{n * num}", rest = "{n - n * num / den}", one_part_too_many = "{n / den * (num + 1)}"), values = list(n = c(12, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 40), num = 1:3, den = 2:6), constraints = c("num < den", "n %% den == 0"), name = "FRA") avg <- item_model( stem = "The heights of {k} plants are {paste(seq(a, by = s, length.out = k), collapse = ', ')} cm. What is their mean height?", key = "{a + s * (k - 1) / 2} cm", distractors = c(sum = "{k * a + s * k * (k - 1) / 2} cm", largest = "{a + s * (k - 1)} cm", divided_by_wrong_n = "{(k * a + s * k * (k - 1) / 2) / (k - 1)} cm"), values = list(k = 3:5, a = c(10, 12, 14, 20), s = c(2, 4)), constraints = "(s * (k - 1)) %% 2 == 0", name = "AVG") speed #> <mv_item_model> SPD #> Stem: A train travels {v * t} km in {t} hours. What is its average speed? #> Key: {v} km/h #> Distractor 1: {v * t * t} km/h (multiplied) #> Distractor 2: {v * t - t} km/h (subtracted) #> Distractor 3: {v * t + t} km/h (added) #> v: 40, 50, 60, ..., 110, 120 #> t: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 #> 45 combinations of values meet the constraints; 45 give items whose options all differ. Printing a model checks it: All 45 combinations of speed and time give four different options. generate_isomorphs() draws items from the combinations and puts the options in random order: x <- generate_isomorphs(speed, n = 3, seed = 15) x$stem #> [1] "A train travels 500 km in 5 hours. What is its average speed?" #> [2] "A train travels 240 km in 6 hours. What is its average speed?" #> [3] "A train travels 540 km in 6 hours. What is its average speed?" as.data.frame(x[, c("id", "A", "B", "C", "D", "key")]) #> id A B C D key #> 1 SPD-01 100 km/h 2,500 km/h 505 km/h 495 km/h A #> 2 SPD-02 234 km/h 40 km/h 1,440 km/h 246 km/h B #> 3 SPD-03 546 km/h 3,240 km/h 90 km/h 534 km/h C The fraction model is less safe. With \(\frac{1}{2}\), the students who chose soccer and those who did not are the same number, so the key and the rest distractor are identical. generate_isomorphs() leaves such combinations out, and says so: fams <- generate_isomorphs(list(speed, frac, avg), n = 12, seed = 151) #> FRA: 25 of 56 combinations of values give two identical options or cannot be computed, and were left out. Add a constraint to rule them out. #> AVG: 2 of 24 combinations of values give two identical options or cannot be computed, and were left out. Add a constraint to rule them out. table(fams$model) #> #> AVG FRA SPD #> 12 12 12 Almost half of the fraction model’s combinations were dropped, and two of the mean model’s. The message is a request to fix the model with a constraint, so that the next person who uses it, or the software, does not depend on the check (Exercise 1). 15.3 Example 2: Calibrating the families The 36 items were field-tested on 800 students. We simulate the responses: Each family has its own difficulty, each item adds item-specific noise with an SD of 0.2 logits, and fractions with a numerator above 1, which take two steps, are 0.8 logits harder than unit fractions. Then we calibrate the Rasch model. # Simulated field test of the generated items: 800 students. set.seed(1515) two_step <- !is.na(fams$num) & fams$num > 1 b_true <- c(SPD = -0.2, FRA = -0.4, AVG = 0.4)[fams$model] + 0.8 * two_step + rnorm(nrow(fams), 0, 0.2) theta <- rnorm(800) resp <- sapply(b_true, function(b) rbinom(800, 1, plogis(theta - b))) colnames(resp) <- fams$id rasch <- mirt(as.data.frame(resp), 1, "Rasch", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE) pars <- tidy(rasch) items <- as.data.frame(fams) b <- pars[pars$term == "b", ] items$b <- b$estimate[match(items$id, b$item)] items$b_se <- b$std.error[match(items$id, b$item)] calibrate_families() summarizes each family. Its observed SD includes the estimation error of each \(b\); with se, the error variance is subtracted, which leaves the within-family SD. The 95% interval is where a new isomorph’s difficulty is expected to fall, and field_n translates the prediction error into the size of a field test that would estimate the item as precisely. cal <- calibrate_families(items, family = "model", se = "b_se") cal #> Item families: 3 families, 36 items; SD within corrected for estimation error #> family items mean_b sd_within 95% for new item field_n isomorphic #> SPD 12 -0.25 0.19 -0.64 to 0.14 135 yes #> FRA 12 0.04 0.46 -0.89 to 0.97 23 NO #> AVG 12 0.51 0.27 -0.04 to 1.07 69 yes #> field_n: Test takers a field test would need to estimate a new isomorph's b as precisely #> as its family mean predicts it. Isomorphic: SD within at most 0.30. The speed and mean families are isomorphic, with within-family SDs of about 0.2 and 0.3 logits: Their family means are worth a field test of 70 to 140 students. The fraction family spreads over almost two logits. Sorting its items by difficulty shows why: fr <- items[items$model == "FRA", c("id", "num", "den", "b")] fr[order(fr$b), ] #> id num den b #> 22 FRA-10 1 6 -0.6857 #> 18 FRA-06 1 5 -0.6532 #> 19 FRA-07 1 5 -0.4371 #> 15 FRA-03 1 4 -0.1901 #> 21 FRA-09 1 6 -0.0803 #> 17 FRA-05 3 4 0.0779 #> 24 FRA-12 2 6 0.1389 #> 13 FRA-01 2 3 0.1877 #> 23 FRA-11 2 6 0.4410 #> 20 FRA-08 3 5 0.4661 #> 16 FRA-04 3 4 0.5483 #> 14 FRA-02 2 3 0.6966 All five unit fractions are easier than all seven others. Splitting the family by that variable gives four isomorphic families (Figure 15.1): items$family <- ifelse(items$model == "FRA", ifelse(items$num == 1, "FRA-unit", "FRA-nonunit"), items$model) cal2 <- calibrate_families(items, family = "family", se = "b_se") cal2 #> Item families: 4 families, 36 items; SD within corrected for estimation error #> family items mean_b sd_within 95% for new item field_n isomorphic #> FRA-unit 5 -0.41 0.26 -0.96 to 0.15 76 yes #> SPD 12 -0.25 0.19 -0.64 to 0.14 135 yes #> FRA-nonunit 7 0.37 0.22 -0.09 to 0.82 106 yes #> AVG 12 0.51 0.27 -0.04 to 1.07 69 yes #> field_n: Test takers a field test would need to estimate a new isomorph's b as precisely #> as its family mean predicts it. Isomorphic: SD within at most 0.30. autoplot(cal2) Figure 15.1: Item families after splitting the fraction model. Dots are items, diamonds family means, and bars the 95% interval for a new isomorph. The split is a substantive finding, not a statistical repair: Finding \(\frac{2}{3}\) of a number takes one step more than finding \(\frac{1}{3}\) of it. The item writers can keep one model and treat num > 1 as a feature, or write two models; either way, the family mean of the original model would have misled. 15.4 Example 3: One step, with a random item effect The two-step approach treats the estimated difficulties as data. A one-step model fits the responses directly: The family is a fixed effect, and each item’s departure from its family mean is a random effect whose variance is \(\sigma^2\), pooled over families. mirt’s mixedmirt() fits it (the estimation takes about a minute): design <- data.frame(family = factor(items$family)) mm <- mixedmirt(as.data.frame(resp), model = 1, itemdesign = design, fixed = ~ 0 + family, random = ~ 1 | items, verbose = FALSE) fixed <- summary(mm, verbose = FALSE)$fixed data.frame(family = sub("family", "", rownames(fixed)), difficulty = -fixed[, "Estimate"]) # mirt models easiness; reverse the sign #> family difficulty #> 1 AVG 0.503 #> 2 FRA-nonunit 0.357 #> 3 FRA-unit -0.370 #> 4 SPD -0.253 sqrt(coef(mm)$items) # within-family SD #> COV_items_items #> par 0.240 #> CI_2.5 0.145 #> CI_97.5 0.306 The family difficulties match the two-step means, and the within-family SD is about 0.24 logits, close to the 0.2 that was simulated. This is the LLTM of Chapter 14 with a random item effect, and the same model fits as a generalized linear mixed model with the eirm package (Bulut et al. 2021), from data in long format. Item features such as num > 1 can go into the same formula: # install.packages("eirm") library(eirm) long <- data.frame(person = rep(seq_len(nrow(resp)), ncol(resp)), id = rep(colnames(resp), each = nrow(resp)), resp = as.vector(resp)) long <- merge(long, items[, c("id", "model", "family")]) long$two_step <- as.integer(long$family == "FRA-nonunit") m_eirm <- eirm("resp ~ -1 + model + two_step + (1|person) + (1|id)", data = long) print(m_eirm, difficulty = TRUE) # family difficulties and the two-step effect lme4::VarCorr(m_eirm$model) # person and within-family item variance With the feature in the model, the original three item models stay, and the fixed effect of two_step estimates how much the second step adds. Hierarchical models of this kind can also give each family its own variance and its own discrimination (Sinharay et al. 2003; Geerlings et al. 2011). 15.5 Example 4: Does the family mean predict new items? The real test of family calibration is a held-out one: Calibrate each family on some of its items and predict the others as if they were new. number <- as.integer(sub(".*-", "", items$id)) old <- items[number <= 6, ] new <- items[number > 6, ] cal_old <- calibrate_families(old, family = "family", se = "b_se") new$predicted <- cal_old$mean_b[match(new$family, cal_old$family)] sqrt(mean((new$predicted - new$b)^2)) #> [1] 0.251 The family means miss the new items by about a quarter of a logit, about what the within-family SDs promised, and three times the standard error of an item calibrated on 800 students. That is precise enough to assemble field-test or practice forms, and to start online calibration, where new items are given as unscored pretest items and their own estimates replace the family mean as responses come in. Whether it is precise enough for scored items on a high-stakes test is a judgment about the decisions the scores support, not a property of the data. 15.6 Your turn Add a constraint to frac so that no combination gives identical options, and print the model. Isomorphic: SD within at most 0.50. The constraint that the four answers are all different leaves 31 combinations. It rules out \(\frac{1}{2}\) (also written \(\frac{2}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{6}\)), where the rest equals the key, and \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{2}{5}\), where the rest equals one part too many. Writing the general constraint is safer than listing the fractions, because it also holds after someone adds new values. Each unit of the numerator adds about 0.4 logits, and the LLTM’s cross-validated error (about 0.28 logits) is close to that of the split families (0.25): The feature does most of the work of the split. It does a little worse because the simulated effect is a step from unit to non-unit fractions, which a straight line in num only approximates. All 216 combinations still give four different options, so the check passes. But a distance of 10 km in 2 hours and one of 1,200 km in 10 hours are not the same task for a Grade 7 student: Larger numbers and less friendly divisions make items harder. Whether they are isomorphs is an empirical question that only a field test answers, and extending the values is a change to the item model that needs one. With 0.5, the original fraction family (0.46) counts as isomorphic. Its interval for a new item then spans almost two logits: Every unit fraction item would be predicted about 0.45 logits too hard, and every other one about a third of a logit too easy. The threshold should come from how precise the family mean must be for its use, not be loosened to pass a family.
