Chapter 16 Automated scoring Learning goals. After this chapter you can explain what an automated scoring engine learns from human scores, and why it is a prediction model of the raters rather than a measurement model; train a simple engine on human-scored text with train_scorer() and judge it on responses it has not seen; evaluate machine scores with exact and adjacent agreement, quadratic weighted kappa, the standardized mean difference and PRMSE, overall and within groups, using agreement_report(); recognize construct-irrelevant features that an engine can reward, and choose how much of the scoring an engine should do; place human raters and an engine on the Wright map with a many-facet Rasch model (rater_facets()), and see what machine scoring does to item thresholds and test scores (scoring_shift()). Key terms: Automated scoring, PRMSE, feature, overfitting and cross-validation, human-in-the-loop, Wright map. 16.1 The ideas Constructed responses, from a one-sentence explanation to a full essay, are scored by trained raters against a rubric. Chapter 8 treated the raters’ scores as data for a polytomous IRT model and checked that two raters agree. Human scoring is slow and expensive, so many testing programs now use an automated scoring engine: A model that predicts the score a trained rater would give. An engine is built the way any machine learning model is (Chapter 13). Each response is turned into features, such as the words it uses, its length, or its spelling, and a model learns from a set of human-scored responses which features go with which scores. The engine never reads the rubric. It learns whatever predicts the raters, including features the rubric does not mention. Two consequences follow: The engine can only be as good as its training scores. If the raters are inconsistent, the engine learns their noise; if they are biased, it learns their bias. Agreement is not the same as measuring the construct. Long answers tend to earn high scores, so length predicts scores, but an engine that rewards length is scoring something other than the rubric. Such features add construct-irrelevant variance and invite gaming. Machine scores are therefore judged against human scores before they are used, following Williamson, Xi and Breyer (2012): Agreement with a human rater: Exact and adjacent agreement and the quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), which should be at least 0.70 and not much below the agreement between two humans (degradation of at most 0.10). Score level: The standardized mean difference (SMD) between machine and human scores, within $$0.15 overall. Fairness: The same SMD within groups of test takers, often within $$0.10, because an engine can match humans overall and still score one group lower (Bridgeman et al. 2012). Agreement with one rater undersells a good engine, because that rater makes errors too. The proportional reduction in mean squared error (PRMSE) asks a better question: How much of the variance of the true score, the average over many raters, do the machine scores explain (Loukina et al. 2020)? It uses the double-scored responses to estimate rater error and corrects for it. A PRMSE of 0.80 means the machine scores predict the true score about as well as a measure with reliability 0.80 would. Finally, a program decides how much the engine does. It can be the sole scorer; a check scorer next to one human read, where a second person reads only the responses on which human and machine disagree; or not be used at all. The stronger the role, the stronger the evidence it needs (Yan et al. 2020). 16.2 Example 1: Training and judging an engine A Grade 7 science test asks: “Why does bread go mouldy faster on the kitchen counter than in the fridge?” A full answer has three key ideas: mould is a living fungus, it grows from spores that are already on the bread or in the air, and warmth speeds its growth while cold slows it. Each answer scores 0 to 3, one point per idea. We simulate 900 answers, all scored by one rater and half of them by a second. Students state each idea in many different ways, and some state an idea wrongly with much the same words (“Cold makes it grow faster.”), which earns no credit. # Simulated short answers to the mouldy bread question, scored 0 to 3. set.seed(1616) pick <- function(...) sample(c(...), 1) ideas <- list( # one function per key idea; each call writes one sentence function() paste0(pick("Mould", "Mold", "The fuzz", "The green stuff", "It"), " ", pick("is a fungus", "is a kind of fungus", "is a living fungus", "is alive, a type of fungus", "is a living thing called a fungus"), "."), function() paste0(pick("Its spores", "Tiny spores", "Mould spores", "Spores"), " ", pick("are already on the bread", "float in the air", "land on the bread from the air", "are everywhere in the air"), pick("", " and start to grow", " and grow on it"), "."), function() paste0(pick("Warmth", "A warm kitchen", "Heat", "Being warm"), " ", pick("speeds up its growth", "makes it grow faster", "helps it grow quickly"), " ", pick("and the cold fridge slows it down", "while cold slows it", "but low temperatures stop it growing fast"), ".")) wrong <- list( # the same ideas stated wrongly, with much of the same vocabulary function() paste0(pick("Mould", "Mold", "The fuzz", "It"), " ", pick("is not alive", "is a kind of plant", "is just dirt", "is not a living thing"), "."), function() paste0(pick("The bread", "The flour", "Old bread"), " ", pick("makes the mould by itself", "turns into mould", "grows the fuzz on its own"), "."), function() paste0(pick("Cold", "The fridge", "A low temperature"), " ", pick("makes it grow faster", "speeds up its growth", "helps mould grow"), ".")) filler <- c("I think this is because of science.", "This happens a lot in my house.", "Bread is made of flour and water.", "It is gross when bread goes bad.") answer <- function(theta) { has <- runif(3) < plogis(1.4 * (theta - c(-1, 0, 0.7))) bad <- !has & runif(3) < 0.4 txt <- c(vapply(ideas[has], function(f) f(), ""), vapply(wrong[bad], function(f) f(), ""), sample(filler, rbinom(1, 2, 0.4))) if (!length(txt)) txt <- "I don't know." list(text = paste(sample(txt), collapse = " "), true = sum(has)) } ans <- lapply(rnorm(900), answer) rate <- function(true) pmin(3, pmax(0, round(true + rnorm(length(true), 0, 0.45)))) bread <- data.frame(id = 1:900, response = vapply(ans, `[[`, "", "text"), true = vapply(ans, `[[`, 0, "true")) bread$human1 <- rate(bread$true) bread$human2 <- ifelse(runif(900) < 0.5, rate(bread$true), NA) Two raters agree well on the double-scored answers. An engine has to do at least this well: head(bread$response, 3) #> [1] "A low temperature speeds up its growth. This happens a lot in my house. The fuzz is a living fungus." #> [2] "Spores float in the air and grow on it. The green stuff is a kind of fungus." #> [3] "Mold is a fungus. Being warm helps it grow quickly while cold slows it. This happens a lot in my house." dbl <- !is.na(bread$human2) agreement_report(bread$human2[dbl], bread$human1[dbl])[, c("n", "exact", "qwk")] #> Machine-human agreement #> n exact qwk #> 458 0.66 0.81 #> Meets: QWK >= 0.7 and within 0.1 of human-human QWK; |SMD| <= 0.15 overall and <= 0.1 within groups (mv_rules()). We train the engine on the first 600 answers and keep the last 300 as a test set that it never sees. train_scorer() fits a ridge regression of the first human score on the words and two-word phrases of each answer, and chooses the amount of shrinkage by cross-validation: train <- bread[1:600, ] test <- bread[601:900, ] engine <- train_scorer(train, response = "response", score = "human1") engine #> <mv_scorer> ridge regression on words and two-word phrases #> 600 responses, 366 features, lambda = 14.7, cross-validated RMSE = 0.51, QWK = 0.87 #> Check it with agreement_report(); use it with predict() or score_open(). head(tidy(engine), 10) #> # A tibble: 10 × 3 #> by term weight #> <chr> <chr> <dbl> #> 1 all fungus 0.451 #> 2 all is a 0.294 #> 3 all spores 0.226 #> 4 all slows it 0.207 #> 5 all slows 0.207 #> 6 all the 0.197 #> 7 all a fungus 0.190 #> 8 all of fungus 0.172 #> 9 all a 0.169 #> 10 all cold slows 0.144 Among the words with the largest weights are the ones the rubric cares about, fungus, spores and slows. Nothing told the engine so; it learned them because raters gave points to answers that used them. But is a and the are near the top as well. They carry no idea; they go with longer answers, and longer answers tend to state more ideas. Now the test set: test$machine <- predict(engine, test) agreement_report(test$machine, test$human1, test$human2) #> Machine-human agreement #> group n n_double mean_human mean_machine exact adjacent qwk qwk_human corr #> All 300 162 1.66 1.67 0.77 1.00 0.88 0.81 0.88 #> smd prmse verdict #> 0.02 0.94 meets #> Meets: QWK >= 0.7 and within 0.1 of human-human QWK; |SMD| <= 0.15 overall and <= 0.1 within groups (mv_rules()). On answers it has never seen, the engine agrees with the first rater at least as well as the two raters agree with each other, its scores are at the same level (SMD near zero), and its PRMSE is above 0.9: It predicts the true score better than a single rater does. On this evidence it could at least serve as a check scorer. Figure 16.1 shows the same statistics as a picture. autoplot(agreement_report(test$machine, test$human1, test$human2)) Figure 16.1: Agreement report for the engine on the test set: QWK with the first rater (dot) next to human-human QWK (cross), and the machine-human SMD with the band of $$0.10. 16.3 Example 2: What is the engine rewarding? Agreement statistics average over the answers in the test set. To see what the engine actually rewards, give it answers whose correct score you know. A rater would give the first two answers below 0, because they name the right words but explain nothing; the third 0, because both its statements are wrong; and the fourth the full 3, because it states all three ideas in words the engine has rarely seen: # Four answers with a known correct score, unlike any in the training data. probe <- data.frame(response = c( "fungus spores cold warm fungus spores grow", "Spores spores spores. Fungus fungus fungus. Warm warm warm.", "The fuzz is not a living thing. Cold makes it grow faster.", "It is a mushroom-like organism whose seeds drift onto the loaf, and it multiplies quicker in heat than in a chilled fridge."), rater = c(0, 0, 0, 3)) probe$machine <- predict(engine, probe) probe$raw <- round(predict(engine, probe, type = "raw"), 2) probe[, c("rater", "machine", "raw")] #> rater machine raw #> 1 0 1 1.10 #> 2 0 1 1.21 #> 3 0 0 0.34 #> 4 3 1 1.08 The engine gets the third answer right: Wrong statements like these were common in the training data, and it learned that not alive and grow faster after cold go with low scores. It gets the other three wrong. It gives a point to each list of key words, which explains nothing, and only one point to the best answer, because that answer is phrased in words the training answers never used. Nothing in the agreement statistics of Example 1 warned about this: The test set held only answers like the training answers, so it could not show what happens with an unusual writer, or when test takers learn how the engine works. This is the core lesson of automated scoring for a psychometrician: agreement with raters is necessary evidence, not sufficient evidence. A validity argument for machine scores also needs to show that the features the engine uses are part of the construct, that the engine treats groups of test takers the same way, and that the scoring design catches responses the engine was not built for. A check scorer design does the last part automatically: Answers on which human and machine disagree go to a second reader. 16.4 Example 3: The engine on the Wright map Agreement statistics are on the score scale of one item. A testing program reports on the logit scale of the whole test, where items are banked and students are scored, and the Wright map (Chapter 7) shows that scale with students and items side by side. An engine can be put on it too, in two ways. The first treats the engine as one more rater. A many-facet Rasch model (Linacre 1989) adds a rater facet to the partial credit model, \[\mathrm{logit}\, P(X_{pir} = k \mid k-1 \text{ or } k) = \theta_p - \delta_{ik} - \lambda_r,\] so each rater \(r\), human or machine, gets a severity \(\lambda_r\) on the same scale as the students’ \(\theta_p\) and the thresholds \(\delta_{ik}\). rater_facets() fits it as an explanatory IRT model with the eirm package (Bulut et al. 2021). With by_item = TRUE each rater gets a severity for each item, the rater-by-item bias terms of a facets analysis. The second asks what machine scores do to the items. scoring_shift() calibrates the same students twice, once with human and once with machine scores, links the two calibrations through items the engine does not score, and compares the thresholds. It also scores every student’s machine-scored answers with the human calibration, which is what happens when a bank calibrated on human scores is used with an engine. We simulate a science test of 600 students with 10 multiple-choice items and three written answers scored 0 to 3. A trained rater reads every answer, a second rater half of them, and an engine all of them. The engine misses one of the ideas on Q2, but you would not know that from its average over the three items. # A test with 10 multiple-choice items and three written answers (Q1 to Q3), # scored 0 to 3 by one or two raters and by an engine. set.seed(1617) n <- 600 theta <- rnorm(n) mc <- data.frame(student = sprintf("S%03d", 1:n), sapply(seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 10), function(b) as.integer(runif(n) < plogis(1.2 * (theta - b))))) names(mc)[-1] <- sprintf("MC%02d", 1:10) read <- function(true) pmin(3, pmax(0, true + sample(c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1), length(true), TRUE))) written <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(j) { true <- rowSums(sapply(c(-1, 0, 1) + c(-0.2, 0, 0.2)[j], function(b) runif(n) < plogis(1.5 * (theta - b)))) machine <- read(true) if (j == 2) { # the engine misses an idea on Q2 miss <- machine > 0 & runif(n) < 0.35 machine[miss] <- machine[miss] - 1 } data.frame(student = mc$student, item = paste0("Q", j), human1 = read(true), human2 = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.5, read(true), NA), machine = machine) })) Each row of written is one answer with its three scores. Fit the facets model with a severity for each rater on each item: fx <- rater_facets(written, raters = c("human1", "human2", "machine"), by_item = TRUE, labels = c("Rater 1", "Rater 2", "Engine")) fx #> Rater facets: 3 raters (AI: Engine), 600 persons, 3 items, severity by item #> #> Rater severity (logits; positive = harsher than the average rater): #> rater ai severity se #> Rater 1 -0.02 0.04 #> Rater 2 -0.07 0.04 #> Engine AI +0.09 0.04 #> #> Flags: #> [BLOCK] rater severity, Engine, Q2: +0.44 logits, SE 0.09. Engine is #> harsher than the human raters here. Overall, the engine is only 0.1 logits harsher than the average rater, well within the range of the two people. Item by item it is not: On Q2 it is about 0.4 logits harsher than the human raters, several standard errors from zero. Figure 16.2 draws the map. The faint points in the rater column are the severities by item, and Q2’s engine point sits apart. gg_wright(fx) Figure 16.2: Wright map with a rater facet: Students (left), the thresholds of the three written answers (middle), and the severity of the two human raters and the engine (right), all on one logit scale. The faint points are each rater’s severity on each item. Now the items. This score is harder to reach when the engine #> scores: It is harsher here than human raters. #> [REVIEW] threshold shift, Q2, threshold 3: +0.46 logits (human 1.20, #> machine 1.66). This score is harder to reach when the engine #> scores: It is harsher here than human raters. All three Q2 thresholds move up by about half a logit when the engine scores (Figure 16.3). A bank calibrated on machine scores would record Q2 as a harder item than it is, and a cut score set on it would move with it. The students’ test scores move less, by about 0.04 SD, because Q2 is one item among 13. A small change in the total does not mean the engine is harmless: It is concentrated on one item, and in Lab 10 it is concentrated on one group of students. gg_wright(sh) Figure 16.3: Wright map of human vs AI scoring: The students’ scores (left) and the thresholds of each written answer (right) from human scores (circles) and machine scores (triangles). Thick lines mark thresholds that move by more than 0.3 logits. Both results can join an audit: ai_audit(components = list(fx, sh)) adds their flags to the checks of Chapter 18. 16.5 Your turn Retrain the engine in Example 1 with length = TRUE, which adds the number of words as a feature. Solutions # 1. adding response length engine_len <- train_scorer(train, length = TRUE) agreement_report(predict(engine_len, test), test$human1, test$human2)[, c("qwk", "smd", "prmse")] #> Machine-human agreement #> qwk smd prmse #> 0.88 0.02 0.94 #> Meets: QWK >= 0.7 and within 0.1 of human-human QWK; |SMD| <= 0.15 overall and <= 0.1 within groups (mv_rules()). tidy(engine_len)[tidy(engine_len)$term == "(length)", ] #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> by term weight #> <chr> <chr> <dbl> #> 1 all (length) 0.0781 # 2. a small training set engine_100 <- train_scorer(bread[1:100, ]) agreement_report(predict(engine_100, test), test$human1, test$human2)[, c("qwk", "smd", "prmse")] #> Machine-human agreement #> qwk smd prmse #> 0.78 0.05 0.79 #> Meets: QWK >= 0.7 and within 0.1 of human-human QWK; |SMD| <= 0.15 overall and <= 0.1 within groups (mv_rules()). # 3. agreement with the second rater d <- !is.na(test$human2) agreement_report(test$machine[d], test$human2[d])[, c("n", "qwk")] #> Machine-human agreement #> n qwk #> 162 0.88 #> Meets: QWK >= 0.7 and within 0.1 of human-human QWK; |SMD| <= 0.15 overall and <= 0.1 within groups (mv_rules()). # 5. one severity per rater rater_facets(written, raters = c("human1", "human2", "machine"), labels = c("Rater 1", "Rater 2", "Engine")) #> Rater facets: 3 raters (AI: Engine), 600 persons, 3 items #> #> Rater severity (logits; positive = harsher than the average rater): #> rater ai severity se #> Rater 1 -0.02 0.04 #> Rater 2 -0.07 0.04 #> Engine AI +0.09 0.04 #> #> No AI rater differs from the human raters by more than 0.3 logits. Agreement does not change, and length gets a small weight. Here the words already carry the key ideas, so length adds little. In real essays length is often one of the strongest predictors, which is why engines that use it need checks for gaming and for groups who write shorter answers. With 100 answers the engine has seen fewer ways of stating each idea, so it misses more of them in new answers: QWK drops by about 0.1 and PRMSE to below 0.8, now no better than a single rater. Engines need hundreds of scored responses per item, and more for long answers. The QWK with human2 is about the same as with human1, although the engine never saw human2. The engine has learned the rubric’s ideas, not the quirks of one rater; an engine that agreed much better with its training rater than with others would be copying that rater’s errors. Chapter 17 Large language models as a colleague Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe what a large language model (LLM) does and why its output varies and can be wrong; use an LLM through mirtverse to draft analysis code, write items and score responses, and see exactly what is sent to it; explain why every LLM output in testing needs a check, and use mirtverse’s checks for wrong keys, weak distractors and machine-human agreement; make LLM work reproducible by recording and replaying responses, and say what to report about an LLM in a technical manual or paper. Key terms: large language model, prompt, hallucination, human-in-the-loop, automatic item generation, automated scoring. 17.1 The ideas A large language model is a neural network trained on a very large amount of text to predict the next piece of text. Given instructions and context, the prompt, it continues them, and that one ability is enough to write items, explain results, score essays against a rubric or draft code. Claude, GPT and the open models that run on a laptop through Ollama all work this way. For a psychometrician, three properties matter more than how the network works: Its output is a sample. The same prompt can give different answers on different runs and with different versions of the model. An LLM is not a function with a fixed value; it behaves more like a rater. It can be fluently wrong. A model can write an item with no correct option, invent a reference or misread a rubric, in the same confident style as a correct answer. Such errors are called hallucinations, and they are found only by checking. What you send leaves your computer. Unless the model runs locally, the prompt goes to a provider. Test content and response data may be confidential, so what is sent has to be a decision, not an accident. These properties lead to the way mirtverse uses LLMs, which is also a good rule for any testing program (Hao et al. 2024; Bulut et al. 2024): The model drafts, something else checks, and a person decides. Generated items are answered again by a second, independent model call that does not see the key. Machine scores must agree with human scores, overall and within groups, before they count, following the framework of Williamson, Xi and Breyer (2012). Anything the model is unsure about goes to a person. mirtverse talks to models through the ellmer package. mv_ask_setup() chooses a provider once: Claude or OpenAI with your own API key, or Ollama for a free model that runs on your own computer. This chapter instead runs in replay mode: mv_llm_replay() answers every request from a file of recorded responses that comes with mirtverse, so the examples need no key, no internet connection and give the same results for every reader. Those responses were written by hand to show what a model returns, including a few deliberate mistakes; they were not produced by a live model. 17.2 Example 1: From a sentence to a tested script mv_ask() turns a plain-language request into an analysis plan and the plan into an R script built from tested templates. The model never writes code and never sees the responses: It sees the request and a summary of the columns. You can see that payload before anything is sent with dry_run = TRUE: # mirt's Science data: 392 respondents, 4 attitude items scored 1 to 4. resp <- Science request <- "Fit a graded response model to these attitude items, check the fit and explain the results." mv_ask(request, data = resp, dry_run = TRUE) #> This would be sent to recorded responses: #> #> Request: Fit a graded response model to these attitude items, check the fit and explain the results. #> #> Data: 392 rows, 4 columns. #> Columns (name | type | distinct values | min | max | share missing | guessed role | categories): #> - Comfort | integer | 4 | 1 | 4 | 0.00 | item | #> - Work | integer | 4 | 1 | 4 | 0.00 | item | #> - Future | integer | 4 | 1 | 4 | 0.00 | item | #> - Benefit | integer | 4 | 1 | 4 | 0.00 | item | The payload holds the request, the number of rows and, for each column, its type, range, share missing and the role mirtverse guesses for it. With anonymize = TRUE the column names are replaced by codes as well. Now the real call, answered from the recording: s <- mv_ask(request, data = Science, ask = FALSE) s$parser #> [1] "recorded responses" s$plan$model #> [1] "graded" s$plan$assumptions #> [1] "All four columns (Comfort, Work, Future, Benefit) are items scored 1 to 4." #> [2] "No grouping column was mentioned, so no DIF analysis is included." #> [3] "Used the 4 columns that look like item responses as items." The model chose the graded response model, kept the default steps, and stated two assumptions it made. Read them: An assumption is where a model fills a gap in your request, and a wrong one gives a wrong analysis that runs without error. The script itself is printed with s, and run with run_script(s). 17.3 Example 2: Writing items, and catching the mistakes The assessment pipeline writes items for the cells of a blueprint. Each multiple-choice item comes with a key and a rationale for every option, and is then checked by a second call that answers it blind. # A two-cell blueprint for a short Grade 7 numeracy quiz. cells <- data.frame(content = c("Ratios and rates", "Measurement"), cognitive = c("Apply", "Apply"), n = c(2, 2)) p <- mv_pipeline("Grade 7 numeracy", verbose = FALSE) p <- set_blueprint(p, cells, construct = "Grade 7 numeracy", use = "classroom diagnostic", population = "Grade 7 students") p <- suppressWarnings(generate_items(p, n = 2)) p$items[, c("id", "stem", "key", "verify_answer", "key_check")] #> # A tibble: 4 × 5 #> id stem key verify_answer key_check #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> #> 1 G001 A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2… A A agree #> 2 G002 A cyclist rides 45 km in 3 hours at a ste… C C agree #> 3 G003 A garden is 12 m long and 7 m wide. How m… A B disagree #> 4 G004 A water bottle holds 2.5 litres. How many… B B agree Two of the four items have problems. The writer keyed the garden item (G003) as 84 m, which is the garden’s area, but the question asks for the fence around it, the perimeter of 38 m. The checking call answered B and the item is flagged. In the millilitre item (G004), one distractor is a length, not a volume, so no test taker would choose it: f <- flags(p, stage = "generation") f[, c("check", "target", "level", "value")] #> # A tibble: 4 × 4 #> check target level value #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> #> 1 key_check G003 block key A, verifier chose B; Fencing a… #> 2 distractor G004 review D (implausible) #> 3 coverage Ratios and rates / Apply review 2 items for a target of 2 #> 4 coverage Measurement / Apply review 2 items for a target of 2 p$items$verify_note[3] #> [1] "Fencing around the garden is the perimeter, 2 x (12 + 7) = 38 m (option B); 84 m is the area, so the key appears to be wrong." A block flag stops the pipeline at the next stage until a person fixes the item or acknowledges the flag. The coverage flags are a reminder that items are lost in review and field testing, so a pool needs more items than the blueprint asks for. Notice what the checks do not do: They do not show that the items measure Grade 7 numeracy, that they are fair, or that their difficulty suits the test. Content review and a field test still do that. Items written one by one also have no family: Each needs its own field test. Template-based generation from item models (Chapter 15) trades variety for items that can be calibrated as a family. 17.4 Example 3: Is a recording reproducible? Replay makes a session reproducible in a strong sense: The same calls on the same data give the same output, on any computer. It also makes the limits of a recording visible. Change the request by one word and the recording has no answer for it: tryCatch( suppressWarnings(generate_items(set_blueprint(mv_pipeline(verbose = FALSE), c(Algebra = 2)), n = 1)), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)) #> [1] "This request is not in the recording examples.json. A recording answers only the exact calls it was made from. Use a live model (mv_llm_replay(FALSE), then mv_ask_setup()), or record the call with mv_llm_record()." For your own work, mv_llm_record("session.json") saves every request and response while you use a live model, and mv_llm_replay("session.json") plays them back. Keep the file with your analysis, as you would keep the data and the code. When you report work that used an LLM, say which model and version you used and when, give the prompts (mirtverse’s are in its source code and in the recording), say what was sent and what was not, and describe how the outputs were checked. Experimental: Language models as respondents. Some researchers ask a language model to answer items as a described person would (“a Grade 7 student who struggles with mathematics”) and treat the answers as a “silicon sample” (Argyle et al. 2023). If that worked, items could be tried out before a field test. simulate_llm_respondents() lets you try it, and compare_synthetic() checks the result against real data. Here twelve personas answer one item from each of the twelve families in itemtext, whose field test gives the real proportions correct (p_field). The recorded answers were written to show the problems that studies of simulated respondents report: items <- itemtext[endsWith(itemtext$id, "-01"), ] personas <- c( "A Grade 7 student who struggles with mathematics.", "A Grade 7 student who struggles with mathematics and is still learning English.", "A Grade 7 student who finds fractions and decimals hard but tries every question.", "A Grade 7 student who often rushes and makes careless mistakes.", "A Grade 7 student who is about average in mathematics.", "A Grade 7 student who is about average in mathematics and is still learning English.", "A Grade 7 student with average marks who is anxious on tests.", "A Grade 7 student who is about average in mathematics and likes word problems.", "A Grade 7 student who is strong in mathematics.", "A Grade 7 student who is strong in mathematics and is still learning English.", "A Grade 7 student in an enriched mathematics program.", "A Grade 7 student who is strong in mathematics but reads slowly.") syn <- simulate_llm_respondents(items, personas) compare_synthetic(syn, setNames(items$p_field, items$id)) #> <mv_synthetic_comparison> 12 simulated respondents, 12 items (EXPERIMENTAL) #> item p_real p_synthetic difference #> N01-01 0.54 1.00 0.46 #> N02-01 0.34 1.00 0.66 #> N03-01 0.62 1.00 0.38 #> N04-01 0.41 0.42 0.01 #> N05-01 0.62 1.00 0.38 #> N06-01 0.39 0.92 0.53 #> N07-01 0.22 0.67 0.45 #> N08-01 0.28 0.17 -0.11 #> N09-01 0.32 0.92 0.60 #> N10-01 0.62 1.00 0.38 #> N11-01 0.36 0.17 -0.19 #> N12-01 0.58 1.00 0.42 #> #> * The simulated respondents find the items easier than real test #> takers: Mean proportion correct 0.77 against 0.44. #> * They order the items by difficulty only loosely like real test takers #> do (Spearman correlation 0.68), so they cannot stand in for a field #> test of difficulty. #> * Their answers vary little: 5 distinct response patterns among 12 #> simulated respondents. Respondents described alike answer alike. #> * Simulated respondents are experimental: Use them to find unclear #> items or to plan a study, not to estimate item parameters or to #> replace a field test. Even “struggling” personas get most items right, so the items look far easier than they are. The short items, such as adding fractions (N06-01) and comparing decimals (N09-01), look easy to the model whatever their real difficulty, and the long word problems look hard. Personas described alike answer alike, and the ones described as “still learning English” miss every long word problem whatever their mathematics: A stereotype, not a measurement. Simulated respondents can help find unclear wording or plan a study. They cannot estimate item parameters, check fairness or replace a field test, and mirtverse labels them experimental for that reason. 17.5 Your turn Run mv_ask(request, data = Science, dry_run = TRUE, anonymize = TRUE). Chapter 18 Validity, fairness and governance of AI Learning goals. After this chapter you can place an AI component in the argument-based approach to validity, and name the threats it adds to each inference; audit an automated scorer with ai_audit(): Agreement with human raters, differential scoring across groups, drift across administrations and DIF on the test as scored; fold the results of difficulty models and item generators into the same audit; draft a validity argument with validity_argument(), and say what evidence no statistic can provide: Human oversight, disclosure and appeals. Key terms: Validity argument, differential scoring, DIF, human-in-the-loop, automated scoring. 18.1 The ideas The earlier chapters of this part each checked one AI component on its own terms: A scoring engine against human raters (Chapter 16), a difficulty model by cross-validation (Chapter 14), an item generator by calibrating its families (Chapter 15). A testing program needs one more step: To ask what the components do to the validity of the scores, for the use the scores are put to. The Standards (American Educational Research Association et al. 2014) apply to AI components as to any other part of a test, and the guidelines of the International Test Commission and the Association of Test Publishers for technology-based assessment (International Test Commission and Association of Test Publishers 2022) add advice on automated scoring, security and accessibility. The argument-based approach (Kane 2013) organizes the evidence. An interpretation-and-use argument is a chain of inferences from a response to a decision, each resting on a claim that evidence must support: Scoring: The score follows the rubric as trained raters apply it. Generalization: The score would be about the same with another occasion, form, rater or engine version. Extrapolation: The score reflects the construct, equally for all groups of test takers. Decision: Using the score for its purpose is appropriate. An AI component adds threats to every link. A scoring engine may reward features that are not in the rubric, such as length or vocabulary (Williamson et al. 2012). It may be retrained or updated by a vendor between administrations, so that a score means something different from one year to the next. It may treat groups differently: Answers that people would score the same may get lower machine scores when they are typed on a phone or written by English language learners. Johnson, Liu and McCaffrey (2022) separate two questions here. Measurement bias asks whether the scores measure the construct equally for all groups, which is the familiar DIF question. Algorithmic bias asks whether the engine predicts the human score equally well for all groups, given the human score. The second is checked by comparing machine and human scores within groups among responses that people scored the same; we call a failure of that check differential scoring. The decision inference is different in kind. It is supported by how the scores are used: Which responses a person reads before a score counts (human-in-the-loop), what test takers are told about automated scoring, how a score can be appealed, and how the component is monitored after it goes live. These are matters of policy and documentation. An audit can show which responses need a person; it cannot show that a person reads them. 18.2 Example 1: Auditing a scoring engine A college uses an automated engine to score two writing prompts, W1 and W2, on a 0 to 4 rubric, for placement into first-year writing courses. Test takers write in a spring or a fall window, on a laptop or a phone. A validity sample of 30% is also scored by a person, and half of those by a second person. We simulate the scores. The engine rewards length, and answers typed on a phone are shorter, so on W2 it gives some phone answers a point less than their true score. A stricter engine version was installed for the fall window, and it marks down some W1 answers. # Simulated machine and human scores of two writing prompts, 2,400 test takers. set.seed(1818) n <- 2400 writing <- data.frame( person = rep(sprintf("P%04d", 1:n), each = 2), window = rep(rep(c("Spring", "Fall"), each = n / 2), each = 2), device = rep(ifelse(runif(n) < 0.3, "Phone", "Laptop"), each = 2), prompt = rep(c("W1", "W2"), n)) theta <- rep(rnorm(n), each = 2) true <- pmin(pmax(round(2 + 1.1 * theta + rnorm(2 * n, 0, 0.5)), 0), 4) noisy <- function(x, p) # off by one point with probability p pmin(pmax(x + ifelse(runif(length(x)) < p, sample(c(-1, 1), length(x), TRUE), 0), 0), 4) writing$machine <- noisy(true, 0.25) short <- writing$device == "Phone" & writing$prompt == "W2" & true > 1 & runif(2 * n) < 0.35 writing$machine[short] <- true[short] - 1 # shorter answers marked down strict <- writing$window == "Fall" & writing$prompt == "W1" & true > 0 & runif(2 * n) < 0.30 writing$machine[strict] <- true[strict] - 1 # the fall engine version read <- rep(runif(n) < 0.3, each = 2) twice <- read & rep(runif(n) < 0.5, each = 2) writing$human1 <- ifelse(read, noisy(true, 0.25), NA) writing$human2 <- ifelse(twice, noisy(true, 0.25), NA) writing$device <- factor(writing$device, levels = c("Laptop", "Phone")) writing$window <- factor(writing$window, levels = c("Spring", "Fall")) The usual first check is agreement with human raters, which agreement_report() gives (Chapter 16): r <- writing[!is.na(writing$human1), ] agreement_report(r$machine, r$human1, r$human2, by = r$prompt) #> Machine-human agreement #> by group n n_double mean_human mean_machine exact adjacent qwk qwk_human #> W1 All 747 369 1.95 1.82 0.60 0.97 0.83 0.86 #> W2 All 747 369 1.98 1.94 0.61 0.98 0.84 0.85 #> corr smd prmse verdict #> 0.83 -0.11 0.78 meets #> 0.85 -0.04 0.80 meets #> Meets: QWK >= 0.7 and within 0.1 of human-human QWK; |SMD| <= 0.15 overall and <= 0.1 within groups (mv_rules()). Both prompts meet the rules. ai_audit() runs this check and the others in one call. The first group of device (Laptop) is the reference group, and the first window (Spring) is the baseline for drift: audit <- ai_audit(writing, human2 = "human2", group = "device", item = "prompt", period = "window") audit #> AI audit: 6 checks, 2 flags (2 block, 0 review) #> check tested flagged status #> human agreement 2 0 ok #> machine agreement 2 0 ok #> overall bias 2 0 ok #> subgroup agreement 4 0 ok #> differential scoring 2 1 BLOCK #> drift 2 1 BLOCK #> #> Flags: #> [BLOCK] differential scoring, W2, Phone: gap -0.19 SD, SE 0.04. For #> responses human raters scored the same, the engine scores Phone #> students lower than Laptop students. #> [BLOCK] drift, W1, Fall: SMD -0.20 against -0.04, QWK 0.79 against #> 0.86. The engine's scores have changed since the first period: #> Check what changed (engine version, prompts, population) and #> rescore if needed. Agreement passes overall and within groups, but two checks block. The differential scoring check compares the machine-minus-human difference of phone and laptop answers that people scored the same: audit$differential #> # A tibble: 2 × 6 #> item group reference n gap se #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 W1 Phone Laptop 217 -0.00220 0.0439 #> 2 W2 Phone Laptop 217 -0.195 0.0441 On W2, the engine scores phone answers about 0.2 SD lower than laptop answers that people scored the same, four to five standard errors from zero. This is what agreement within groups can miss: Phone users may also score lower in truth (here they do not), so a lower mean alone proves nothing, while a gap at the same human score is the engine’s. The drift check compares each window with the first: audit$drift[, c("item", "period", "n", "smd", "qwk", "smd_change", "p_change", "drift")] #> # A tibble: 4 × 8 #> item period n smd qwk smd_change p_change drift #> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <lgl> #> 1 W1 Spring 400 -0.0418 0.863 NA NA FALSE #> 2 W1 Fall 347 -0.200 0.788 -0.159 0.000391 TRUE #> 3 W2 Spring 400 -0.0451 0.859 NA NA FALSE #> 4 W2 Fall 347 -0.0349 0.825 0.0102 1 FALSE In the fall, W1’s machine scores fell to 0.2 SD below the human scores, and agreement dropped. A drift flag needs both a change larger than the rule and a change beyond sampling error; p_change is Bonferroni-adjusted across the items and windows tested. Figure 18.1 shows the three score checks. autoplot(audit) Figure 18.1: The score checks of the audit. Dashed lines are the default limits; bars are 95% confidence intervals. When the test as scored is available, responses adds a DIF analysis with dif(). DIF on an AI-scored item is flagged for review; DIF on an item the engine does not score is reported for information, because it belongs to content review, not to the engine. Lab 10 does this. 18.3 Example 2: Other AI components The same audit takes the results of the tools of the earlier chapters. Here a difficulty model was trained with the proportion correct of the field test among its features, and one of three item families is not isomorphic: # Simulated field-test results of 45 items from three item models. set.seed(181) fam <- rep(c("Ratios", "Fractions", "Equations"), each = 15) b <- c(Ratios = -0.8, Fractions = 0, Equations = 0.9)[fam] + rnorm(45, 0, rep(c(0.1, 0.1, 0.5), each = 15)) items <- data.frame(id = sprintf("I%02d", 1:45), family = fam, b = b, b_se = 0.08, words = round(25 + 5 * b + rnorm(45, 0, 6)), p_field = round(plogis(-1.2 * b + rnorm(45, 0, 0.05)), 3)) model <- predict_difficulty(items, c("family", "words", "p_field"), se = "b_se", methods = "lltm") families <- calibrate_families(items, family = "family", se = "b_se") ai_audit(components = list(model, families)) #> AI audit: 2 checks, 2 flags (1 block, 1 review) #> check tested flagged status #> leakage 3 1 BLOCK #> isomorphism 3 1 REVIEW #> #> Flags: #> [BLOCK] leakage, p_field: rank correlation with b -0.99. A feature #> this close to the label is probably computed from the same #> responses: Leave it out. #> [REVIEW] isomorphism, Equations: SD within 0.46. The family mean is #> not a good estimate for new items from this item model. The leaked feature blocks: Its predictions would vanish for new items that have no field test (Chapter 14). The family that is not isomorphic is flagged for review: Its mean is a poor stand-in for new items’ difficulties (Chapter 15). 18.4 Example 3: From audit to argument validity_argument() turns the audit into a draft argument. Each inference gets its claim, the threats an AI component adds, the evidence from the audit and a status: va <- validity_argument(audit, construct = "academic writing in English", use = "placement into first-year writing courses", population = "incoming students") va[, c("inference", "status")] #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #> inference status #> <chr> <chr> #> 1 Scoring supported #> 2 Generalization threatened #> 3 Extrapolation threatened #> 4 Decision needs evidence cat(format(va, "markdown")) #> The argument for using academic writing in English scores for placement into first-year writing courses, with automated scoring of constructed responses, by the four inferences of the argument-based approach (Kane, 2013). #> #> ### Scoring (supported) #> #> - **Claim:** Scores from automated scoring of constructed responses follow the scoring rubric as trained human raters apply it. #> - **Threats:** The engine rewards surface features (length, vocabulary, spelling) rather than the ideas in the rubric; human scores used to train or check it are unreliable. #> - **Evidence:** Human agreement: 2 tested, no flags. Machine agreement: 2 tested, no flags. Overall bias: 2 tested, no flags. #> #> ### Generalization (threatened) #> #> - **Claim:** Scores would be the same on another occasion, form, rater or engine version, so they mean the same across administrations. #> - **Threats:** An engine update, a new prompt or a change in the population shifts machine scores; agreement holds in one year only. #> - **Evidence:** Drift: 2 tested, flagged W1, Fall [SMD -0.20 against -0.04, QWK 0.79 against 0.86]. #> - **To do:** Resolve the flags, then rerun the audit before the scores are used. #> #> ### Extrapolation (threatened) #> #> - **Claim:** Scores reflect academic writing in English, and do so equally for all groups of incoming students. #> - **Threats:** Features unrelated to the construct, such as language proficiency, lower machine scores for some groups; DIF on AI-scored items. #> - **Evidence:** Subgroup agreement: 4 tested, no flags. Differential scoring: 2 tested, flagged W2, Phone [gap -0.19 SD, SE 0.04]. #> - **To do:** Resolve the flags, then rerun the audit before the scores are used. Not checked yet: DIF. #> #> ### Decision (needs evidence) #> #> - **Claim:** Using the scores for placement into first-year writing courses is appropriate, with the human oversight, disclosure and appeals the use requires. #> - **Threats:** Machine scores are used without human review where stakes are high; test takers are not told how they were scored; errors cannot be appealed. #> - **Evidence:** None yet. #> - **To do:** Document human review of flagged and low-confidence responses, disclosure to test takers, and an appeals process. No audit can supply this evidence. The scoring inference is supported: The engine agrees with people as well as they agree with each other. Generalization and extrapolation are threatened by the fall engine version and by the phone gap. The decision inference needs evidence whatever the audit finds, and the draft says what: Human review of flagged responses (here, W2 answers typed on a phone, and all fall W1 answers until the engine is fixed), disclosure to test takers that their writing is scored by a machine, and a way to appeal. The argument can go into the HTML report of the calibrated test with mv_report(), as one more section: mv_report(fit, file = "writing-report.html", extra = list("Validity argument" = va)) 18.5 Governance An audit at launch is not enough. A testing program that uses AI components should also decide, and write down, the following. The Standards (American Educational Research Association et al. 2014) and the ITC/ATP guidelines (International Test Commission and Association of Test Publishers 2022) ask for most of it in general terms. Ownership. Who is accountable for each component, including one bought from a vendor, and who may change it. Change control. Every new engine version, prompt or training set is audited on a validity sample before it goes live, as Example 1 shows why. Human oversight. Which responses a person reads: A share chosen at random for monitoring, every response the engine is unsure about, and any group or item where the audit found a problem until it is fixed. Disclosure and appeals. Test takers and score users are told how scores were produced, and a score can be rescored by a person on request. Monitoring. The audit is rerun on each administration, with its results in the technical report. Data. What test-taker data a component sees, where it is processed, and how long it is kept, especially when a language model runs on a provider’s servers (Chapter 17). Guidance on AI in testing is moving quickly. The checks in this chapter rest on long-standing psychometric principles, but the regulations and professional guidelines that apply should be checked at the time of use. 18.6 Your turn Rerun the audit of Example 1 with mv_rules(subgroup_smd = 0.25). The college would place phone users lower than their writing warrants on W2, and every fall W1 test taker lower than a spring one with the same answer. A rule should be set from the size of a difference that matters for placement, before the data are seen. The phone gap on W2 is found (in a smaller sample, so with a wider interval); drift cannot be checked, because there is only one window. An audit can only find problems its data can show: Version changes need data from before and after. Its checks table shows one prompt tested instead of two. A validity sample must include every group and item the scores will be used for, in numbers large enough to detect a gap that matters. Chapter 19 Knowledge graphs and IRT Learning goals. After this chapter you can describe what a test measures as a knowledge graph of concepts, prerequisites and items, and build one with mv_kg_build() or as_mv_kg(); check a graph for problems with mv_kg_check() and draw it with gg_kg(); read a graph’s Q-matrix and list the mastery patterns its attribute hierarchy allows; turn a graph into a confirmatory multidimensional IRT model with mv_kg_model() and mv_kg_irt(), and test the graph’s claims against simpler and stricter models; check a graph against data with mv_kg_fit() and explain item difficulty with it using mv_kg_explain(). Key terms: Knowledge graph, Q-matrix, attribute hierarchy, multidimensional IRT, likelihood-ratio test. 19.1 The ideas Every test is built on claims about what it measures. A blueprint says which content each item covers; a curriculum says that some ideas must be learned before others; a teacher knows that an item about subtracting mixed numbers also needs borrowing. Most of these claims stay in documents and heads. A knowledge graph writes them down in a form a computer can check and a model can use. It has three kinds of parts. Concepts (also called skills, attributes or objectives): What the test is meant to tell us about. Relations between concepts. The most useful is prerequisite of: Equivalent fractions before adding fractions with unlike denominators. Prerequisite edges point forward in the learning order and should never form a cycle. A weaker relation, related to, links concepts where neither comes first. Items, each linked to the concepts it measures. These links are the rows of the Q-matrix (Tatsuoka 1984): One row per item, one column per concept, with a 1 where the item needs the concept. The graph connects two traditions in psychometrics. In multidimensional IRT, the Q-matrix is the loading pattern of a confirmatory model: Each concept is a factor, and an item has a slope only on the concepts it measures (Chapter 4). In cognitive diagnosis, the same Q-matrix says which skills an item needs, and prerequisite edges form an attribute hierarchy (Leighton et al. 2004; Templin and Bradshaw 2014): A student can master a concept only after mastering its prerequisites, so some mastery patterns are impossible. Knowledge space theory (Doignon and Falmagne 1999) builds a whole theory of assessment on such structures. A graph is a set of claims, and each claim can be wrong. An item can be linked to the wrong concept, a prerequisite can be missing or reversed, and two concepts can be impossible to tell apart because the same items measure them. The work in this chapter is to make the claims explicit, check what can be checked without data, and then let the data speak. 19.2 Example 1: A graph for fraction subtraction Tatsuoka’s fraction subtraction data are the best-known real data in cognitive diagnosis: 536 middle school students answered 20 items such as \(4\frac{1}{3} - 2\frac{4}{3}\), and the items were coded on eight attributes (Tatsuoka 2002; DeCarlo 2011; Torre and Douglas 2004). mirtverse stores the responses as fraction_subtraction and the Q-matrix as a knowledge graph, fraction_subtraction_kg. resp <- fraction_subtraction kg <- fraction_subtraction_kg kg #> <mv_kg> Fraction subtraction (Tatsuoka): 8 concept(s), 20 item(s) #> Edges: 0 prerequisite, 0 related, 56 measures tidy(kg) #> # A tibble: 28 × 6 #> node kind label description links depth #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 convert_whole concept Convert a whole number to … Attribute … 3 0 #> 2 separate_whole concept Separate a whole number fr… Attribute … 13 0 #> 3 simplify_first concept Simplify before subtracting Attribute … 3 0 #> 4 common_denominator concept Find a common denominator Attribute … 5 0 #> 5 borrow_whole concept Borrow from the whole numb… Attribute … 8 0 #> 6 column_borrow concept Column borrow to subtract … Attribute … 2 0 #> # ℹ 22 more rows The graph has eight concepts and 20 items, with 56 item-to-concept links. No prerequisite edges were published with the Q-matrix, so the graph has none yet. tidy() counts the items linked to each concept (links). subtract_numerators is needed by 19 of the 20 items, while column_borrow is needed by only two. Before any data are used, mv_kg_check() looks for problems in the structure itself. mv_kg_check(kg) #> <mv_kg_check> 0 block, 1 review, 0 info #> * [review] few_items: column_borrow is measured by 2 item(s); at least #> 3 are needed to estimate it as its own dimension. The check finds one thing to review: Two items are too few to estimate column_borrow as its own dimension. A concept that nearly every item needs, like subtract_numerators, has the opposite problem: It is hard to separate from overall proficiency. Neither is an error in the graph, but both limit what a model can learn about these concepts. gg_kg(kg) Figure 19.1: The fraction subtraction graph: Eight attributes on the left, each joined to the items that need it. Now suppose a mathematics teacher states two prerequisites as hypotheses: Borrowing from the whole number needs the whole number to be separated from the fraction first, and column borrowing needs subtracting numerators. We add these edges to the same concepts and items. concepts <- tidy(kg) concepts <- concepts[concepts$kind == "concept", ] kg_h <- mv_kg_build( concepts = data.frame(concept = concepts$node, label = concepts$label), edges = data.frame(from = c("separate_whole", "subtract_numerators"), to = c("borrow_whole", "column_borrow")), items = mv_kg_qmatrix(kg), name = "Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites") kg_h #> <mv_kg> Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites: 8 concept(s), 20 item(s) #> Edges: 2 prerequisite, 0 related, 56 measures #> Learning order (by prerequisite depth): #> 0: convert_whole, separate_whole, simplify_first, common_denominator, subtract_numerators, reduce_answer #> 1: borrow_whole, column_borrow The print-out now gives a learning order. The hierarchy has a practical consequence: With eight concepts there are \(2^8 = 256\) possible mastery patterns, and each prerequisite rules out the patterns where a concept is mastered without its prerequisite. patterns <- mv_kg_hierarchy(kg_h) nrow(patterns) #> [1] 144 attr(patterns, "possible") #> [1] 256 Two edges remove 112 of the 256 patterns. A diagnostic model that respects the hierarchy has fewer classes to estimate, and the hierarchy itself can be tested by comparing models with and without it. 19.3 Example 2: From graph to IRT model mv_kg_model() writes the confirmatory mirt model a graph implies, and mv_kg_irt() fits it. Eight correlated dimensions on 536 students is a large model that takes many minutes to fit, so we work with a smaller graph: The three concepts with the clearest roles, separating the whole number, borrowing, and finding a common denominator. mv_kg_subset() keeps these concepts, the prerequisite between two of them, and the 16 items that need at least one of them. kg3 <- mv_kg_subset(kg_h, c("separate_whole", "borrow_whole", "common_denominator")) kg3 #> <mv_kg> Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites: 3 concept(s), 16 item(s) #> Edges: 1 prerequisite, 0 related, 26 measures #> Learning order (by prerequisite depth): #> 0: separate_whole, common_denominator #> 1: borrow_whole q <- mv_kg_qmatrix(kg3) resp3 <- resp[rownames(q)] spec <- mv_kg_model(kg3) cat(attr(spec, "item_syntax")) #> separate_whole = FS04, FS05, FS07, FS09, FS10, FS11, FS13, FS14, FS16, FS17, FS18, FS19, FS20 #> common_denominator = FS01, FS02, FS03, FS05, FS13 #> borrow_whole = FS04, FS10, FS11, FS13, FS17, FS18, FS19, FS20 #> COV = separate_whole*common_denominator, separate_whole*borrow_whole, common_denominator*borrow_whole Each concept is a factor, and each item loads on the concepts its row of the Q-matrix names; items that need two concepts load on both. By default all concepts correlate. The structure argument changes that: structure = "graph" lets only concepts joined by an edge correlate, a strict reading of the graph in which concepts without an edge are unrelated. m_uni <- mirt(resp3, 1, verbose = FALSE) m_graph <- mv_kg_irt(kg3, resp3) m_strict <- mv_kg_irt(kg3, resp3, structure = "graph") anova(m_uni, m_graph) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> m_uni 7739 7775 7793 7876 -3838 #> m_graph 7371 7421 7447 7564 -3641 394.115 13 0 anova(m_strict, m_graph) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> m_strict 7641 7689 7713 7825 -3778 #> m_graph 7371 7421 7447 7564 -3641 273.888 2 0 Two comparisons answer two questions. Against a single dimension, the three-concept model fits far better: The likelihood-ratio statistic is about 394 on 13 degrees of freedom, and BIC drops by more than 300. The items measure more than one proficiency, in the way the graph describes. Against the strict model, the correlated model also wins clearly: Finding a common denominator has no edge in the graph, yet it correlates with the other two concepts. round(summary(m_graph, verbose = FALSE)$fcor, 2) #> separate_whole common_denominator borrow_whole #> separate_whole 1.00 0.77 0.37 #> common_denominator 0.77 1.00 0.38 #> borrow_whole 0.37 0.38 1.00 Separating the whole number and finding a common denominator correlate at about 0.77, much more than the two concepts the teacher linked (about 0.37). This is a typical finding, not a failure: A prerequisite edge says something about the order of learning, and concepts that are learned in the same lessons correlate whether or not one is a prerequisite of the other. The correlations are a reason to look again at the graph, for example to ask whether a related-to edge is missing. The fitted model is an ordinary mirt model, so everything from the earlier chapters works on it, and the graph travels with it. pars <- tidy(m_graph) head(pars[pars$estimate != 0, ]) #> # A tibble: 6 × 5 #> item itemtype term estimate std.error #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 FS01 2PL a2 5.14 NA #> 2 FS01 2PL d 1.08 NA #> 3 FS02 2PL a2 7.39 NA #> 4 FS02 2PL d 2.30 NA #> 5 FS03 2PL a2 13.8 NA #> 6 FS03 2PL d 0.943 NA attr(m_graph, "mv_kg") #> <mv_kg> Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites: 3 concept(s), 16 item(s) #> Edges: 1 prerequisite, 0 related, 26 measures #> Learning order (by prerequisite depth): #> 0: separate_whole, common_denominator #> 1: borrow_whole as_mv_kg() also goes the other way: Given any confirmatory mirt model, it reads the loading pattern back into a graph, which is a quick way to draw a model you already have. 19.4 Example 3: Checking the graph against data The comparisons above test the graph as a whole. mv_kg_fit() looks for the places where the data disagree with it. For each item, it asks whether the item agrees more with another concept than with its own: It correlates the item with the rest score of every concept, corrected for how reliable each rest score is. For each pair of concepts, it turns the factor correlations of the correlated model into partial correlations, the correlation of two concepts once the others are held constant. Concepts that are directly related keep a clear partial correlation; concepts related only through others do not. We can pass in the model we already have. check <- mv_kg_fit(kg3, resp3, model = m_graph) check #> <mv_kg_fit> Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites: 3 concept(s), 16 item(s), N = 536 #> 1 review, 0 info #> * [review] missing_relation: separate_whole and common_denominator have #> no edge but a partial correlation of 0.73, and their items are about #> equally hard; add a related edge? tidy(check, "relations") #> # A tibble: 3 × 10 #> concept_a concept_b edge from to type r partial ease_a ease_b #> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 separate_whole common_d… none <NA> <NA> <NA> 0.771 0.733 0.487 0.500 #> 2 separate_whole borrow_w… sepa… sepa… borr… prer… 0.372 0.130 0.487 0.410 #> 3 common_denomina… borrow_w… none <NA> <NA> <NA> 0.383 0.164 0.500 0.410 No item is flagged: Every item agrees best with a concept it is linked to. The relation evidence makes the earlier observation precise. Holding borrowing constant, separating the whole number and finding a common denominator still have a partial correlation of about 0.73, while the teacher’s prerequisite (separate_whole -> borrow_whole) drops to about 0.14. Because the two concepts’ items are about equally hard, the suggestion is a related edge rather than a prerequisite. gg_kg_fit(check, items = "all") Figure 19.2: The evidence on the three-concept graph: Partial correlations next to each pair, and the suggested related edge as a dashed line. mv_kg_refine() would add the edge. Whether to do so is a content question: Both skills come up when students handle mixed numbers with unlike denominators, so a related edge is plausible, but the data alone cannot say why the concepts go together. A graph also makes claims about difficulty. mv_kg_explain() fits an explanatory Rasch model with the eirm package (Bulut et al. 2021) in which the graph predicts each item’s difficulty: One difficulty per concept (a linear logistic test model, with a random item effect for what the concepts leave unexplained), or the item’s depth in the learning order. explain <- mv_kg_explain(kg, resp) explain #> <mv_kg_explain> Fraction subtraction (Tatsuoka): Item difficulty explained by concepts #> 20 items, N = 536. The graph explains 88% of the item variance. #> label difficulty se p.value #> convert_whole 2.10 0.29 <0.001 #> separate_whole -0.18 0.23 0.42 #> simplify_first -0.40 0.33 0.22 #> common_denominator 1.32 0.24 <0.001 #> borrow_whole 2.33 0.29 <0.001 #> column_borrow -0.01 0.33 0.98 #> subtract_numerators -1.69 0.22 <0.001 #> reduce_answer 0.11 0.28 0.70 #> Items the graph predicts poorly: FS09 (-0.91). The eight attributes explain most of the differences in item difficulty. Borrowing from the whole number and converting a whole number to a fraction add the most difficulty, and subtracting numerators, which almost every item needs, the least. The teacher’s two prerequisites, in contrast, say little about difficulty: mv_kg_explain(kg_h, resp, predictors = "depth") #> <mv_kg_explain> Fraction subtraction with two prerequisites: Item difficulty explained by learning-order depth #> 20 items, N = 536. The graph explains 64% of the item variance. #> label difficulty se p.value #> Learning-order depth 0.47 0.49 0.3353 #> Number of concepts 0.63 0.21 0.0024 Items that need more attributes are harder, but once that is taken into account, an item’s depth in the teacher’s learning order adds little. A prerequisite that does not show up as a difference in difficulty is not necessarily wrong, but it is a claim the data do not support yet. 19.5 Your turn Add a third hypothesis to kg_h: Converting a whole number to a fraction (convert_whole) is a prerequisite of borrowing (borrow_whole). How many mastery patterns are left? Add a cycle by also making borrow_whole a prerequisite of separate_whole. What does mv_kg_check() report, and what happens to mv_kg_hierarchy()? Fit the three-concept model with structure = "orthogonal". How does it compare with the correlated model, and what does that say about scoring the three concepts separately? Draw kg3 with gg_kg(), highlighting common_denominator. Which items does it share with separate_whole? Solutions # 1. a third prerequisite edges3 <- data.frame(from = c("separate_whole", "subtract_numerators", "convert_whole"), to = c("borrow_whole", "column_borrow", "borrow_whole")) kg_h3 <- mv_kg_build(data.frame(concept = concepts$node, label = concepts$label), edges = edges3, items = mv_kg_qmatrix(kg)) nrow(mv_kg_hierarchy(kg_h3)) #> [1] 120 # 2. a cycle kg_cyc <- mv_kg_build(data.frame(concept = concepts$node), edges = rbind(edges3, data.frame(from = "borrow_whole", to = "separate_whole")), items = mv_kg_qmatrix(kg)) mv_kg_check(kg_cyc) #> <mv_kg_check> 1 block, 1 review, 3 info #> * [block] cycle: Prerequisite edges form a cycle through #> separate_whole, borrow_whole, so no learning order exists. #> * [review] few_items: column_borrow is measured by 2 item(s); at least #> 3 are needed to estimate it as its own dimension. #> * [info] isolated: simplify_first has no relations to other concepts. #> * [info] isolated: common_denominator has no relations to other #> concepts. #> * [info] isolated: reduce_answer has no relations to other concepts. try(mv_kg_hierarchy(kg_cyc)) #> Error : The prerequisite edges contain a cycle; see mv_kg_check(). # 3. uncorrelated concepts m_orth <- mv_kg_irt(kg3, resp3, structure = "orthogonal") anova(m_orth, m_graph) #> AIC SABIC HQ BIC logLik X2 df p #> m_orth 7642 7689 7712 7822 -3779 #> m_graph 7371 7421 7447 7564 -3641 276.827 3 0 # 4. shared items gg_kg(kg3, highlight = "common_denominator") q[q[, "common_denominator"] == 1 & q[, "separate_whole"] == 1, ] #> separate_whole common_denominator borrow_whole #> FS05 1 1 0 #> FS13 1 1 1 Borrowing now needs both separating and converting, so more patterns are ruled out: 120 of the 256 remain. The check reports a cycle block flag: Separating the whole number would have to come both before and after borrowing, so no learning order exists. mv_kg_hierarchy() stops with an error, because a cycle allows no consistent set of patterns. The orthogonal model fits much worse than the correlated one (the likelihood-ratio statistic is about 277 on 3 degrees of freedom). The concepts share a lot of variance, so three separate scores would repeat much of the same information; reporting them separately needs care (Chapter 12). Two items, FS05 and FS13, need both concepts; FS13 also needs borrowing. The other common denominator items (FS01 to FS03) involve no whole numbers. Items that load on two concepts help the model separate the concepts from their correlation. B Adapting the book for your course The book is meant to be changed. Each chapter is a separate R Markdown file, each example starts from one data chunk, and the book builds with one command, so you can reorder chapters, replace examples with your own data, or add a chapter for a topic you teach. The files All sources are in the book/ folder of the mirtverse repository: Table B.1: Source files of the book. File Contents index.Rmd Title page and preface 00-author.Rmd About the author 01-measurement.Rmd to 12-reporting.Rmd The twelve chapters, one per course week 13-ml-lens.Rmd, 14-item-text.Rmd, 15-aig.Rmd, 16-auto-scoring.Rmd, 17-llms.Rmd, 18-ai-validity.Rmd The chapters on AI in measurement 90-datasets.Rmd, 91-adapting.Rmd The appendices _bookdown.yml Chapter order (rmd_files) and output folder _output.yml Look of the HTML, PDF and EPUB editions latex/ Title page, preamble and box styles of the PDF edition cover/ Cover artwork and how to regenerate it _common.R Code run before every chapter: Loads mirtverse and sets chunk options references.bib References cited in the book The chapter files and their ids ({#measurement}, {#irt-models} and so on) are kept stable, so links to a chapter keep working across versions. Every chapter has the same shape A Learning goals box. Key terms, linked to the glossary. The ideas. Example 1 and Example 2, each starting with a data chunk labelled data-<chapter id>-1 or -2. Your turn, with solutions in a folded <details> block. In the lab and Further reading. Keep this shape when you add a chapter, and students will always know where to look. Swapping in your own data To use your own data in an example, replace the body of its data chunk and keep the label and the object names listed in Appendix A. For example, to run Example 1 of Chapter 2 on your own dichotomous test: ```{r data-irt-models-1} # Our midterm: 40 multiple-choice items, scored 0/1. resp <- read.csv("midterm-scored.csv")[, -1] # drop the ID column ``` The rest of the example then runs on your data. Two caveats: Examples built on simulated data compare estimates with the true values used to simulate them (objects such as true, true_theta or the planted DIF items). With real data there is no truth, so delete those comparisons or turn them into questions for students. The prose describes the original results. Re-read the text around each output after you swap the data, and edit the interpretation to match. The mirtverse instructor toolkit automates these steps, for example copying a chapter into a course folder and replacing a data chunk; see the instructor toolkit guide. Building the book Install bookdown once, then build from the book/ folder: install.packages("bookdown") bookdown::render_book("index.Rmd") # the whole book, into _book/ bookdown::preview_chapter("05-fit.Rmd") # one chapter, faster Open _book/index.html in a browser to read the result. The whole book builds in a few minutes on a laptop. To publish your own version, put the _book/ folder on any web server, or use GitHub Pages as the mirtverse repository does (its book workflow builds the book and publishes it next to the package website). Suggesting changes Every page has a Suggest an edit link at the top, which opens the chapter’s source on GitHub. Corrections and new examples are welcome as issues or pull requests in the mirtverse repository.
